subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries were before the house last week I promised that at the conclusion of negotiations which were taking place here in Ottawa among Canada, Japan and the United States for the revision of the north Pacific fisheries convention I might be able to make a statement to the house.
At the opening session of the Ottawa negotiations I expressed the hope on behalf of the Canadian delegation that this third meeting of the parties to the international north Pacific fisheries convention would resolve the remaining differences and would culminate in a successful conclusion of the protracted negotiations. Three weeks of uninterrupted negotiations have brought the parties very close to agreement, but it has not been possible to reconcile all the remaining differences, and the delegations have agreed to a recess in the discussions in order to study and recommend to their respective governments other approaches to the unsolved problems.
We had hoped that final agreement could have been reached for the revision of the existing convention which, of course, continues in force but which may be terminated upon 12 months' notice by one of the parties. At the same time we realize that the problems with which the delegations have been faced are very complex, and that all must be solved before agreeing on a convention which we hope will remain in force for many years. The frank and co-operative attitudes of the delegations have permitted much progress and encourage us to hope that we shall reach agreement at our next meeting.
20220-545J
I should like to give, for the information of the house, a very brief rdsumd of the Canadian position. The salmon runs to our streams are of the very highest importance to the fisheries of Canada's Pacific coast. We believe that through scientific study, strict regulation and positive fish culture methods we have maintained these stocks which would otherwise have disappeared. We believe that the salmon resource can be greatly increased by the application of scientifically based techniques which are now emerging. But this maintenance and increase of the runs require not only that we continue our intensive efforts in research, regulation and culture, but that we also continue, at considerable cost to our economy, the protection of our rivers from other uses which would make them unsuitable for salmon. To justify all these costs of maintaining and, we confidently expect, increasing the salmon resources the benefits must accrue to the Canadian economy.
During the past three weeks much progress has been made toward agreement which would meet our needs in an acceptable manner. It seems that, on the one hand, the basis for the Canadian position is now well understood and is given sympathetic consideration. On the other hand we realize that recognition of our special interests must be contingent on continuation of our special efforts to maintain and increase the salmon stocks and on continued full utilization by our fishery, and that the situation must therefore be subject to review by the commission established by the convention. We have been very close to agreement which would embody these essential points.
The greatest unsolved problem is concerned with conservation measures for those stocks of North American salmon which now are fished on the high seas. Although the problem applies especially to sockeye of Alaska origin, Canada has a potential interest in a solution which could be applied to other stocks fished on the high seas although to a much more minor degree. We are also concerned by the growing scientific evidence that the high seas fishing of salmon stocks which are intensively fished inshore may be wasteful.

North Pacific Treaty
It appears that we are close to agreement on a formula which would be acceptable in so far as the major halibut producing areas are concerned. This formula would recognize the long history of research and regulation by the international Pacific halibut commission on behalf of the governments of Canada and the United States, and the resulting successful restoration and maintenance of the important halibut fishery. We had hoped that similar protection could be extended to other areas where the stocks have been the subject of similar study and regulation and are utilized by our fishermen. This must now be a matter for further discussion.
Regarding herring, we hope that a satisfactory solution can be reached as herring is not of significant importance to Japan.
To conclude, I am satisfied that the Canadian delegation, to whom I am very grateful, has put forward its best efforts to bring about agreement which would provide the greatest measure of protection to those Pacific coast fisheries which are the mainstay of our fishing industry in British Columbia. I am also encouraged by the valuable progress that has been made toward the solution of the remaining differences, and hope that these may finally be reconciled at the next meeting.

subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no doubt the house listened with interest to the rather lengthy statement of the minister on this very important subject. I regret that it was not quite as reassuring as we might have hoped it would be, because it is obvious that agreement has not been reached as yet on terms under which the north Pacific fisheries treaty could be extended for another lengthy or indefinite period of time. The minister neglected to say how long this recess in negotiations is going to be, but I hope it will not be too lengthy and that negotiations can be recommenced at an early date.
The problem is, of course, that there is a conflict of interest between Japan on the one hand and the United States and Canada on the other, because Japan depends on high seas fisheries and has very few streams which contribute anything to the stocks of salmon which are commercially exploited in the north Pacific. I would hope that the Canadian delegation, as they no doubt did, pointed out to Japan the possibility of Japan developing artificial spawning beds and other means whereby that country itself might make a worth-while contribution to these stocks of
IMr. Robichaud.]
fish, based on methods that have been developed in Canada.
We will look with interest to the reconvening of negotiations on this treaty, and we assume there will be no possibility of any of the parties giving notice that they intend to withdraw. The minister did not specifically say so, but we would hope that these negotiations will be reconvened at an early date and that a satisfactory agreement will eventually be reached.

subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it will also be recalled that at the time the minister's estimates were before the house we predicted that there would be a postponement or delay in the progress of the discussions and that for a number of reasons, possibly the pending election in the United States, there would not be a desire to announce anything bad arising out of the discussions. I hope we are wrong. I hope our fears will not be borne out when the talks are reconvened, and that the results of the resumed negotiations will be beneficial.
The minister's statement as I heard it was very revealing in that he made no reference whatever to the abstention principle contained in the present treaty. This was the basic point of the treaty negotiated in 1953, namely that Japan would abstain from fishing for certain fish in a certain area of the Pacific ocean. Japan, of course, has objected to this, and it is the main obstacle to the course of orderly discussions that might lead to an agreement. I interpret the minister's failure to make any reference to the abstention principle to mean in effect that perhaps Canada has relaxed what the minister called the firm position of the government in these negotiations, and that if we finally get a treaty we may very well end up with one renegotiated in such a way that the abstention principle is watered down or adulterated or not referred to at all.
As the New Democratic party has consistently pointed out, there is no doubt that we must approach our high seas fisheries from the point of view of international cooperation to conserve those fisheries in order to ensure that fish remain for future generations, and to ensure that exploitation is carried on within limits prescribed by the principles of a scientific approach to conservation itself. It is also a fact that Japan is not the only nation bordering upon the Pacific ocean that fishes in those waters. The Soviet union has an almost rapacious demand for fish products, and in the past few years has expanded tremendously its fishing oper-

ations beyond the area close to their shores where it has traditionally fished.
I would reiterate the vital importance of this matter. To go back to the time before this government were elected to office, they promised that Russia would be drawn into the treaty. It is vitally important to make some approach to the Soviet union to ask that country if they will take part in the next negotiations, even if only in the capacity of an observer. I say this because it is important to have an international agreement among all the nations that are exploiting this particular fishery; and unless Russia does come into the treaty we could very easily see all our efforts toward conservation come to naught because of the expansion of the Soviet union into the high seas salmon fishery.
We shall look forward with great interest to the resumption of these discussions, even though the minister neglected to say when they would be resumed. We hope they will be resumed at an early date and will proceed rapidly to a successful conclusion.

Mr. Speaker, we hope the length of the negotiations that have been carried on is an indication of the desire of the Canadian delegation to safeguard Canada's vital interests at all costs. I would not like to think it is an indication of failure. I prefer to think of it as showing that the minister and the Canadian delegation are determined to maintain our position and insist on the safeguards we have enjoyed in the past.
So far as the west coast is concerned, this is a matter of tremendous importance. The minister is aware of all the representations that have been made on this matter, and though he made no reference to the abstention principle that is included in the present treaty, I trust that at least the idea of it will be carried out even if it is not stated.
We in this party also regret that the statement has not been more conclusive and definite, but we look forward to the resumption of these talks in the not too distant future in order that these problems may be ironed out and a satisfactory agreement signed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MB. KNOWLES-TIME SPENT ON QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I do so entirely on my own responsibility, but I believe that members generally will agree it is a point of privilege and that it concerns all of us as members and that it concerns the house itself.
On April 20 of this year the house, by unanimous decision, adopted certain provisional standing orders and certain guide lines respecting the asking of questions on orders of the day. The immediate result of that decision of the house on April 20 was that for the first few weeks that followed we cut in half the amount of time we had been taking with respect to questions on orders of the day. I think members will agree also that during that period not only did the asking and answering of questions take a shorter period of time, but it was a crisper and better period in every respect.
In recent weeks, however, to put it mildly we have been slipping. I have been keeping my own records, and I have checked with those who keep the official records. We are just about back to where we were before we made the changes on April 20. I have been tempted several times in the last couple of weeks to raise a point of order during the question period because I felt a certain member was abusing the rules by his question or a certain minister was abusing the rules by his answer. However, it really does not help to solve the problem by intervening in that way. I have therefore taken this opportunity to raise this point of privilege.
I suggest that both the house and Your Honour would like us to get back to the

position we achieved immediately after April 20. There is no point in trying to put blame on particular persons. I think in the first place the responsibility and blame rests upon us as members, and that includes all of us. In the second place, I think Your Honour would not mind if I were to say that you have not been clamping down in recent weeks as you were immediately after April 20. You have been reluctant to enforce the rules and the guide lines which the House of Commons placed in your hands. Therefore, on this question of privilege, I believe the house would welcome Your Honour applying more strictly the rules and guide lines we gave you. We would welcome it if they were applied to party leaders and backbenchers alike; we would welcome them being applied to those who ask questions as well as to those who answer them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MB. KNOWLES-TIME SPENT ON QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
On this question of privilege, which I think is not a question of privilege at all, I should like to say that if each member of this house is to give instructions to the Speaker I would be inclined to suggest that questions of privilege should be valid questions; otherwise they should not be raised.
I do not see in what way this can be interpreted as a question of privilege. Had the rights and privileges of members been interfered with, there might be a question of privilege involved; but all the hon. member has done in this instance is draw attention to what he calls a question of privilege in an attempt to place the house in a strait-jacket, according to his ideas, and restrict the privileges of hon. members to ask questions on the orders of the day. We have that restriction applied on Wednesday of each week and Mr. Speaker has rather carefully followed that rule. On the other days there has been no restriction imposed. It is only the hon. member's own opinion that conditions are less favourable now than they were in the last ten days of April; it is not an opinion shared by other hon. members of this house.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to have bogus questions of privilege raised, as this one is, this destroys the effectiveness of the House of Commons. I think people who are raising questions of privilege of this nature should make very sure in advance that they have valid questions of privilege; otherwise I think the hon. member should be interrupted in the course of his remarks, which he has used on this occasion

just to promote an idea that may reside within his mind and that of some of the members of his party, namely that restrictions should be placed on the House of Commons. The restrictions might very well start with the hon. member himself and members of his party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not yet in a position to give the house a precise answer as to the whereabouts of Mr. Hal Banks, although while I am on my feet I am in a position to answer a question put to me recently by the right hon. gentleman which asked when gross negligence in dealing with Mr. Banks first occurred.
I am now in a very clear position to state positively that if there has been gross negligence it started in 1958, when the Department of Justice asked the R.C.M. Police to investigate in order to determine whether Banks had been employing intimidation or violence in the furtherance of union activities. By the end of 1958 information had been obtained about the Walsh beatings. On February 23, 1959, when there was still time to look into the matter of whether Banks could be deported and deprived of Canadian domicile, there had been sent to the minister of justice a full account of the conspiracy to beat Walsh as related by the principal crown witness at the trial, Richard Greaves. On June 14, 1961 there had been sent to the minister, and therefore to the government, another report which included an account of the Walsh conspiracy of the other principal crown witness, Sheehan.
No action was taken against Banks, notwithstanding that this was a time when evidence relating to the Walsh incident was readily available and evidence relating to other incidents might also have been obtained. This was also the time when firm action might have prevented the deterioration in the situation on the St. Lawrence and great lakes system which culminated in the physical impasse on the St. Lawrence seaway in the summer of 1962, when the Welland canal was blocked as described in the Norris report.
Instead, a royal commission was appointed on July 17, 1962. Without detracting from the value of that inquiry it is a fact that an inquiry was not necessary to bring to light the evidence upon which the recent conviction of Banks depended. Thus, these proceedings could have been commenced five years before they were commenced.

Some days ago the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, referring to certain allegations made by individuals who had demonstrated outside R.C.A..F. station La Macaza over Labour day week end relating to unnecessary use of force by R.C.A.F. guards in removing them from the roadway at the entrance to the station, asked the Prime Minister if a further investigation would be made into these allegations.

As hon. members are aware, in reply to a question asked earlier the associate minister had stated that a report had been received from the commanding officer of the station, and that on the strength of that report he was satisfied that no unnecessary use of force had been employed.
Subsequently the associate minister personally interviewed the commanding officer of R.C.A.F. station La Macaza. He was informed by the commanding officer that strict instructions had been given to all R.C.A.F. personnel that the minimum amount of force should be used to remove demonstrators who were blocking entrance to that station and, as far as he and other officers and and noncommissioned officers were aware, these instructions had been complied with.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Canadian
economy is now in its fourth year of advance and is moving strongly ahead. The rise in Canada's gross national product this year surpasses even the 6.6 per cent increase of 1963. Employment so far this year is up 4 per cent from the same period a year ago. Despite a more rapid expansion of the labour force, there are fewer people without jobs.
The general advance has been widely diffused throughout all major segments of industry and all geographic regions. Output in secondary manufacturing industries has continued to grow, service trades and construction have been more active and substantial gains are also being realized in resource industries.
Canada's 1963-64 crop year, which ended July 31, was the most successful wheat marketing year in the nation's history. It was a record year for production, exports and income, in each case well above previous highs. It is a year that will be difficult to match.
A number of importing countries have harvested large crops this year. Nevertheless the outlook for wheat exports is favourable. Canadian wheat is ideally suited for blending with the indigenous soft wheats produced in these countries. Agreements concluded with mainland China and several eastern European countries assure a continuing heavy movement to these markets. Forward sales for the current crop year are encouraging. In short, 1964-65 is going to be a good year for exports of wheat.
Internationally, economic conditions remain generally good, with world production

Supply-Trade and Commerce and trade moving steadily higher. Sales of Canadian products have been more than holding their own in international markets. Rising exports have played a major role in Canada's current expansion. For the period 1960 to 1963 Canada's merchandise exports rose by 30 per cent or nearly 10 per cent each year, and so far this year they are up by a spectacular 23 per cent from the same period in 1963. Even exclusive of wheat, exports are up by 17 per cent. Items contributing in a major way to this increase include lumber, pulp and paper, iron ore, base metals, aircraft and automotive products. Especially encouraging is the further growth in a wide assortment of manufactured goods which, as a group, are assuming increasing importance in Canada's export trade. Canadian manufacturers continue to break new ground in terms of both the broader range of products sold and the growing number of markets penetrated. A significant part of this growth in sales of manufactured goods consists of capital equipment sold under long term financing arrangements of one kind or another, either insurance or direct financing by the government under the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. All major foreign markets have absorbed more Canadian products this year. Exports to the United States are up by 11 per cent, to Britain and the rest of the commonwealth by 21 per cent, to the European economic community by 25 per cent, to Japan by 18 per cent.
The encouraging state of Canada's trade at present does not, of course, mean that those concerned with its promotion can now rest comfortably on their oars. There is nothing static about foreign competition for international trade, and in our promotion activities we look to the years ahead. Moreover, prosperity presents its own special challenges. It is, for example, anomalous but true that Canada's economy is perhaps more vulnerable to external imbalance in good times than in bad. I think the comment that was made today on the orders of the day, that there was some adverse change in our current account balance, was simply an indication that we were very prosperous.
This year's accelerated growth in the Canadian economy accompanied by sharply expanded capital expenditure programs has entailed a new upsurge in import demands. So far in 1964 merchandise imports are up by 19 per cent and payments for non-merchandise items are also up sharply. Thus, the virtually unprecedented rise in export earnings this year has scarcely been adequate to meet the
8630	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce rise in foreign payments. Consequently our current account balance, which last year showed the smallest deficit-about $500 million-in the last nine years, has shown no further improvement this year. Figures recently released by the dominion bureau of statistics show a current account deficit of $518 million for the first half of 1964 compared with a deficit of $452 million for the same period last year. A moderate improvement in the merchandise trade balance has been more than offset by higher net payments on non-merchandise items; in other words, the trade surplus has again grown fairly substantially but it has been offset by these invisible items. These developments illustrate how important it is, even in present conditions of mounting prosperity, to push resolutely ahead with programs to extend our productive capabilities on the basis of competitive efficiency and to develop new markets. It is against this background of solid accomplishment but continuous challenge that the department is pursuing its role of helping to pave the way and to stimulate an ever-increasing flow of Canadian products into the markets of the world, wherever they are to be found.
I would now like to say a word about international trade relations. We are in one of those periods of transition where old trading patterns gradually give way to new. No country can afford to ignore the currents or to lag behind in adapting itself to the changes that are taking place. Especially is this so in the case of Canada, where the further development of our trade and the growth of our economy require that we should exploit every opportunity to gain access to wider markets. Better access to the United States and other markets could, in many cases, provide the necessary incentives for longer production runs and increased specialization, which are so necessary to many of our secondary industries. Improved access would also open up possibilities for the development of new products and for the initiation of new export trade.
The intensive phase of GATT trade and tariff bargaining gets under way in November. While there was some lull in the preparatory work in August, meetings of experts are now being resumed in Geneva with the objective of clearing away remaining difficulties in time for the November 16 deadline. On that date the participating countries are scheduled to begin their detailed bargaining behind closed doors.


The Canadian tariffs and trade committee has now pretty well completed its initial task of receiving briefs and conducting consultations with various Canadian interests. The interest shown by the business community has been most encouraging. More than 400 separate briefs have been received by the tariffs and trade committee. The committee has been going non-stop all summer-like parliament- in receiving interested groups which have been asked for hearings. Our delegation, under the chairmanship of Mr. Norman Robertson, will be entering the negotiations in Geneva better briefed on the views and interests of the various Canadian groups than ever before. The tariffs and trade committee here in Ottawa, under the able and experienced leadership of Mr. Hector McKinnon, will be available as may be required to provide a vital and continuing link between our negotiations in Geneva and the Canadian business community. Some of our negotiating team has already left for Geneva for the final preparatory phase of the negotiations. We expect that the full delegation will be on the ground after the end of the year.
I would not try at this stage to predict the duration of these negotiations, or the final outcome. They will be of great importance to the international trading community and we can expect them to be long and difficult. The task ahead and the challenge the negotiations present fully justify the time and effort required. Special efforts will be necessary to ensure a meaningful negotiation in the agricultural sector. Canada's interests in the negotiations are positive and clear. It is through the opening up of markets on the broadest possible basis that our own trade and economic interests can best be served. In the process concessions will be required in return for benefits received. Our participation will be carefully developed in the light of the national interest and the opportunities presented. We shall be striving for maximum Canadian advantage. As I have said on some other occasions, we shall be tough but not reluctant bargainers.
A most important task of the I960's is to reinforce the efforts of the less developed countries to improve the lot of their peoples and to reach the point of self-sustaining growth. The United Nations trade and development conference laid bare the magnitude of the task and the urgency of the demands of the less developed world. The conference also laid the basis for carrying the work forward through new international machinery devoted exclusively to the problems of trade

and economic development. The Kennedy round of negotiations provides an early opportunity to assist the developing countries through better trade access. The major trading nations, including Canada, have agreed that maximum efforts should be made to open up trading opportunities for the developing countries. Special procedures are being worked out to ensure that the interests of the less developed countries are kept fully in mind.
The United Nations general assembly this autumn has the trade problems of the developing countries high on its agenda. The GATT countries will be having a special session this autumn in Geneva-I expect that my deputy minister will be attending as the chairman of GATT-devoted especially to possible changes in the international trading framework designed to take better account of the trade needs of the developing countries. Canada has played, and will continue to play, its full part in these endeavours.
It is no small achievement that during this period of pause, when the leading trading nations have been preparing themselves for further progress in the direction of international trade and economic co-operation, restrictionist pressures have on the whole been resisted by our trading partners. While some problems of access have been encountered, these have been the exception and Canada's exports to the United States, Britain, the European economic community and Japan have all been running at record levels.
Japan has now become Canada's third largest market and the prospects are for even higher import requirements for the years ahead. The pace at which Japan has been opening up its market to import competition may at times give rise to impatience. Nevertheless, Japan has moved a long way in the last several years. Japan herself has had trouble in gaining improved access to markets for its products. Of key importance is that the movement has been in the direction of freeing up trade and not away from international economic co-operation.
We have been doing well in the British market. Canned apples were freed from import controls in June, and very few of the United Kingdom post-war trade restrictions now remain. I am glad to see that my hon. friend who formerly had responsibility in this matter is smiling, because I know from his experience and from my own how many years it has taken to get rid of canned apples.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Hear, hear.

We are actively pursuing with the British authorities the question of better access for our fresh apples and pork products.
The department has of course followed developments in the United States with particularly close attention. Certain important sectors of our trade have been the object of protectionist pressures, notably oil and lumber, but restrictive measures have been avoided. We are frankly disappointed that the United States has, so far, not felt able to free up the trade in lead and zinc, particularly during this period when the market has strengthened. Lack of substantial progress in easing the United States restrictions on Canadian cheese is equally disappointing. And we are determined that the objectives of our automotive program should be achieved. It is easy to harp at the United States, and we have our problems. But it is important to keep in mind the extent to which new trade restrictions have been avoided and the great potential which exists for expanded trade and fruitful economic co-operation with our major trading partner, the United States.
In its external trade promotion work, the department is building purposefully upon the foundations established by past projects such as the national export trade promotion conferences, the regional trade promotion meetings, and the various sample shows. Those imaginative projects stimulated greater interest in exporting, identified opportunities and potentialities, and pointed to ways and means of capitalizing on them. They induced a gratifying extra momentum to the export activity of our business community.
Our task is always to service expanding interest in export trade, to exploit gains which have been made, as well as to broaden and diversify the base of our trade in continuing to seek new prospects and to avail ourselves of additional export possibilities as these are discovered. As the pattern of our trade develops, new methods must develop with it. The guiding work principle is "promotion in depth"-intensive, detailed, painstaking effort. In particular, attention is being paid to export development for secondary manufactures. Our export manufacturing base is widening in a most encouraging way. As instances of success at export multiply, more and more businessmen are gaining confidence in their competitive capacity in world markets.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Whether it be in our dealings with individual firms or with trade associations; in the bent of our trade missions program or the purpose of our trade fairs program; in the establishing of further regional offices within Canada or new trade posts outside our country; in special activity such as our efforts to encourage the export of Canadian consultant engineering services or our work in developing the export of Canadian-made components needed by overseas industries; in selling bulk or packaged foodstuffs and other agriculture or fishery products or in exporting industrial raw materials or manufactured products-in every area we are working intensively and with purpose. Canadian businessmen are responding to the opportunities and to the challenges in a most gratifying way.
The department's aim is to remain flexible, responsive to fresh opportunities. Prospects, trends and potentialities are kept under constant review. We are constantly adapting to new environmental changes, new developments, and we shall continue to do so.
In our efforts at external trade promotion we are co-operating fully with all provincial trade departments and I am glad to say they are reciprocating in like degree. In matters of mutual interest and concern there is sensible exchange of views at the planning stage, practical collaboration in the organizational phase, effective joint effort at time of execution. I am satisfied that much mutual benefit has already accrued. Indeed, when I first met with the ministers and my opposite numbers in the provincial governments I said I thought that this cooperation was a very good example of cooperative federalism. My officials and their opposite numbers in the provinces have developed intimate and effective relationships that augur well for the future.
In that other important sector of our promotion work, tourism, there is every indication that the Canadian tourist industry will achieve another record year in dollars earned from visitors to this country. The tourist bureau is working to a three year development plan designed to bring tourist earnings to a total of a billion dollars in 1967. This will require a very considerable effort and investment. Good progress is being made and I am confident that the imagination and determination being shown will yield results of which we as Canadians can all be proud.
Hon. members will be interested in the program called "Project Hospitality" which

the travel bureau inaugurated through the Canadian tourist association. Project hospitality consists of a series of seminars and local hospitality conferences in every province aimed at the operator or service level. The objective is to raise the standards of reception and service provided to our visitors. Results to date are very encouraging.
Through the annual federal-provincial tourist conference to be held in Ottawa in November and by continual, almost daily, consultation with the provinces and the transportation companies covering all kinds of promotion activities, the travel bureau continues to provide leadership and a means of co-ordinating promotion of travel in Canada both at home and abroad.
As regards Expo '67, good progress has been made and the corporation advises that preparations are on schedule and prospects for foreign and domestic participation most satisfactory. Hon. members have had an opportunity to be briefed on the striking plans which have been developed for federal and provincial participation in this great centennial event.
A number of questions have been raised regarding the relationships between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the new Department of Industry. They were raised particularly on the estimates of the Department of Industry. There is no need for any confusion on this matter. Those relationships are precisely similar to those existing with the departments of agriculture, fisheries, forestry and mines and technical surveys. The prime responsibility for matters affecting export trade and trade promotion rests with the Department of Trade and Commerce. To the extent that the Department of Industry is successful in increasing productivity, improving the competitive strength of Canadan industry and expanding the range and volume of Canadian industrial production, it will develop new fields of opportunity for export trade development. Officials of the two departments are working in the closest collaboration; their efforts are complementary and mutually reinforcing.
As hon. members are aware, I have responsibility as Minister of Trade and Commerce for a number of boards, crown corporations and agencies which report to parliament through me, but which are not part of the department as such. When we come to the votes covering the estimates of these boards and agencies I shall be pleased to comment or to answer any questions. At this stage I

should like to refer briefly to the operations of the dominion bureau of statistics and the national energy board.
Hon. members will be asked to approve a small sum to undertake preliminary work for the quinquennial 1966 census which will again be taken for Canada as a whole as it was in 1956. The questions to be asked for the population will be limited, as was the case in 1956, to some five basic questions- age, sex, marital status, relationship to head of household and whether living on a farm- plus a question on type and tenure of each occupied dwelling. For agriculture, questions will be asked about the number and size of holdings, type of farm, crop acreages, number of livestock and farm machines and limited information on expenditures.
Since I announced our national power policy to the house a year ago, the board has been engaged, directly and in association with other agencies, in various studies bearing on the implementation of that policy. As the house is aware, the board is also responsible for advising the government on the progress of the national oil policy. Earlier this year I expressed the view that average Canadian production of crude and equivalents should reach about 850,000 barrels a day in 1964. It now appears that this level will be very nearly achieved and that the industry will enjoy an increase of the order of 7 per cent over last year or more than 50 per cent above the level of average production in 1960.
The adjustments inherent in any such program require the constant participation by the board in discussions with companies in the industry, but I think the difficulties have so far been met by the industry and the board with a remarkable degree of success, both in terms of the adaptation of the patterns of the industry within Canada, and in terms of orderly development of the markets in the United States for Canadian oil. The process has not been painless and difficulties remain, but the industry is certainly to be congratulated on what it has so far achieved.
In closing my remarks I should like to stress again the need for Canada to respond appropriately to the basic shifts in the world trading environment that is taking place. Canada is a great trading nation. To maintain and improve our prosperity and our standard of living we must consolidate and improve our position as an international trader.
In the months ahead we can expect keener competition at home and abroad in our efforts to maintain and expand markets for primary products and for secondary manufactures.
Supply-Trade and Commerce We should set our sights on meeting this keener competition, and on adjusting our posture and improving our efficiency to take advantage of broader markets. We must remain competitive if we are to maintain and expand our place in the Canadian market and in the markets of the world. I am confident that Canadian industry can and will respond to the new opportunities and new challenges.

I am not a shorthand writer and he has the advantage of a text, which he follows rather closely, copies of which we have not received. I again draw his attention to a request made by members on this side, as well as on all sides of the house, to the effect that if members of the cabinet are presenting statements and do so from a lengthy and involved text, they should exercise the courtesy of providing party leaders or representatives with copies. After all, the reading of a text by a minister in opening a discussion on his estimates is done with the tolerance of the members of the house and the Chair. Otherwise, if we want to follow the rules strictly, the minister would have to make such a statement spontaneously without a text. If you will permit me to digress slightly, Mr. Chairman, I think this is perhaps one area where things could be improved. Either we should accept the fact that a minister is going to make a statement from a text and have

Supply-Trade and Commerce copies distributed, or the minister should follow the rules and get along without a text.
Be that as it may, I found the minister's statement this afternoon, at least at the beginning, to be rather generalized, and that it painted a picture in rather glowing colours. There was an unfortunate dearth of what one might call hard figures, comparing the progress this year with progress of the past. I should have liked to hear a great deal more detail about what he foresees for the future, and I will deal with that subject more extensively at a later time.
In following the minister's statement I made an attempt to compare it with a speech he delivered to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce annual meeting in Winnipeg on September 28. The two statements were made within a short period of time, and naturally the facts existing on the one occasion cannot be separated from the facts which existed on the other. These facts would not change. Therefore we find a similarity of thought expressed in both statements.
It is interesting to observe that the notes of caution I intend to make this afternoon may be in contrast to what the minister intended in the opening remarks of his statement. What I say is certainly not in the spirit of doom and gloom, which we have observed on the part of his colleagues who were formerly on this side of the house. Though the minister was not here then, I am sure he would blush if he heard or read some of the statements that were made then, in view of some of the things he said in his Winnipeg speech. I should like to quote from that speech, where he said:
The Canadian economy is now in its fourth year of uninterrupted advance and substantial gains are being made this year.
It is too bad the hon. member for Essex East and a few of his fellow gloomsters of the past three years were not in attendance to hear this glowing report in respect of the nature of the economy as it stands today.
The minister has indicated a need for action in certain areas, and I think we should underline these areas. Certainly during the past six or seven years there has been a considerable increase in both exports and imports, but there is a question arising in respect of whether there will be a sufficient increase in exports to more than counterbalance the increase in imports. Is the increase in exports going to be sufficient to even keep pace with the vastly increasing payments on the foreign accounts, which have to be made on the noncommodity side, for interest, dividends and


repayments? We know that from 1946 and 1947 to 1955 and 1956 there was a continuous and fantastic deficit on both the commodity and non-commodity side. There was a surplus on the commodity side I think in 1952, but that is the only exception.
Those deficits in international accounts were made up, so far as we were concerned, and this is what tended to keep the Canadian dollar at an artificially high level for a period of time. The deficits were actually invested in Canada but not necessarily in new investments. A good deal of the deficits were invested in other than new investments and we observed a good deal of purchases in industry made in Canada by foreign interests. These purchases were not all made by United States interests, but by other foreign interests as well. However, the more of this foreign investment there is as the result of a deficit in the international account, the more we must face up to the fact that we are going to have to repay this in some way in the future. Every time we borrow money on the foreign market we must take into account the fact that we are going to have to repay it.
Year by year we see this non-commodity item gaining on us. In fact, the situation is almost similar to a treadmill. This is the price we must pay for the progress that is being made in this country. I am not suggesting this is entirely wrong, but we must realize that this is a price we must be prepared to accept. If we ignore that fact I think we are guilty of very careless thought.
The minister referred to the export of apples from Halifax to the British market. Just as an aside, I should like to point out that I noticed a statement on one of the financial pages of a local daily newspaper which pointed out that the major processor of Ontario apples into apple juice is under British control. Instead of exporting our apples over to Great Britain they have taken over control of this processing industry and process them here.
I should like now to refer again to the speech made by the minister in Winnipeg. I have noted that from 1960 to 1963 exports on the commodity side increased by 30 per cent and that up to this time this year they are-in Winnipeg the minister used the word "whopping".
Spectacular.

Spectacular. I think we all realize that wheat and wheat products have a good deal to do with this, but there are other things. I hope that later the minister

will be able to put on record the increase in sales of natural gas, because there has been quite a considerable advance. It has not been so much in the case of oil, although there has been good maintenance of that market. I intend to discuss the national oil policy.
With regard to the Kennedy round and GATT I believe my colleague, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, will be taking up that subject later. There are also other aspects of the minister's speech and responsibilities that some of my other colleagues will comment upon. Certainly the operations of Eldorado will come under the scrutiny of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona or I miss my guess.
I have the text here of the minister's speech in Winnipeg, and I think that the minister will agree, as will members generally, that there has been a very healthy development in that the increase in the volume of our exports, both as to quantity and as to price, has been in manufactured goods. I think it would have been necessary for us to pause and look at the situation much more closely if this had not been the case. If the increase were limited to basic or prime products then we would merely say that we were continuing and expanding our career of being hewers of wood and drawers of water.
I suggest to the minister that a good deal of the progress has been the result of the programs of really accentuated trade promotion that took place five or six years ago and extended into 1960 and 1961. I was a little disappointed that the minister, when speaking of trade promotion and trade conferences, did not indicate that there were any plans for a repetition of the very successful conference, confrontation, or whatever you want to call it, of our trade commissioners and members of Canadian industry. This took place on the largest possible scale in 1961 or late 1960. I think it certainly revitalized a whole section of the minister's department. I believe it has led to an entirely different atmosphere and has created a feeling of cooperation which has resulted in a large number of regional trade conferences between men in business and officials of the minister's department. It has led to greater co-operation between the federal Department of Trade and Commerce and the various provincial departments of trade and industry.
I would hope that the minister could announce that before long there is going to be another of these rather large gatherings, because as I participated in that conference
Supply-Trade and Commerce I was able to observe the reaction of businessmen from western Canada, particularly from the province of Alberta, and many of our trade commissioners that this was the dawn of a new day. I do not say that conferences of this kind are necessary every year or every second year, but five years will soon have elapsed and I think another one is now called for.
Competition at the international level today is so acute that if Canada is not only to maintain its position but also to go forward there must be a really active, hard sell. People will not come here to buy. They will not walk in on their own. There must be aggressive selling. People can be brought here but they must be encouraged. I wish to congratulate the Department of Trade and Commerce and the minister for having maintained some of the momentum, but I do not think there has been quite the same momentum and I should like to see it picked up.
In Winnipeg the minister warned that unfortunately there has not been the same rate of progress from 1963 into 1964, that is, the same sort of optimistic upturn in our external accounts. There has been a great deal of capital spending which, as he says, has resulted in a resurgence of import demands. The fine increase on the export side has been matched by an increase in imports. If we leave wheat sales aside the 17 per cent increase on merchandise account is matched by a 17 per cent increase in merchandise imports.
But again I come back to the point that there has also been a very significant increase in the non-merchandise account, and it is the non-merchandise account that is most worrisome and the sector over which we have the least control. In the minister's address I noted the following sentence:
It is not unusual that we should continue to experience a sizeable balance of payments deficit on current account in circumstances of rapid expansion such as now prevail. I have no doubt that a deficit of present proportions can be financed without difficulty.
Right away I ask: But for how long can we continue in this position and what has really been the price of past deficits? This is what concerns me. It may be that in a single year we can finance such a deficit without an undue drain on our foreign exchange holdings, but on the other hand it cannot be said that we can continue to do this. It seems to me that all too often we take the easy way out, like the man who is slowly going bankrupt and pays off his shortfall accounts by merely selling his assets. Eventually he will
8636	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce run out of assets and then he comes up against the startling reality that he is bankrupt. This is something we must guard against.
The minister indicated that the aim of his department was to improve and to extend the Canadian industrial structure, and to do this not by restrictive measures but by maintaining a suitable economic climate by the right kind of incentives and by the promotion of exports. Well, I am just wondering. We have noticed that this year, in the second quarter, there has been a levelling off. I am hoping that the minister has been discussing this levelling off with his colleague, the Minister of Finance. Every time there is an upward drive in the cost of production of manufactured goods, the problem of our export trade becomes more difficult.
I would say immediately that one of the restrictive measures involved in so far as export trade is concerned was the imposition of a sales tax on machinery entering into production. I have not at any time been able to see the justification for the imposition of this tax on production machinery when we are trying, with all our might and main, to drive up our exports. I do not know of any other country that has done this. Surely to goodness this is something that I hope the minister will be able to take care of in discussion with his colleague.
I wonder if the hon. member, while he is making this point, would discuss the implication of the 43 per cent increase in exports in June, which is during the period to which he has referred?

The increases are not looked at month by month because it takes just a mere accident of shipping or certain other things to influence the comparison on a month to month basis. I could perhaps say that the 43 per cent would be accounted for by the hurry to complete the wheat deliveries. There may be a number of factors. If the minister is talking about a 43 per cent increase in June of this year as compared with June of last year, then that is a short space because you can see increases or decreases of perhaps 100 per cent from one day to the next.

I was just commenting on the statement the hon. member had made, that during this period there was some slackening of exports. I was pointing out that June was the largest monthly increase we had had in the whole year.

I said there had been a sort of levelling off, not a slackening or a drop.


There is a levelling off. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister perhaps some of the conclusions that have been drawn from the reports issued by the dominion bureau of statistics, in so far as the gross national product is concerned and a few other things that perhaps go to counter balance some of the glowing statements the minister made at the beginning. I should like to cite from a commentary made on the situation which appears in this morning's financial press:
A midsummer slump in business activity may have dimmed hopes for a balanced federal government budget this year.
The gross national product showed no advance in volume in the second quarter, a 1 per cent increase in value, to an annual rate of $46 billion, being matched by a 1 per cent rise in prices. The non-farm output of goods and services dropped in volume by about one half of 1 per cent.
The fall in non-farm production, the first since early in 1961, was accompanied by a slackening in consumer demand, a build-up of manufacturing inventories and a 1 per cent decline in corporation profits.
I am not saying we are on the eve of a disaster. However, I want to point out that there are certain things which we cannot ignore, and we must not go around with our heads in the clouds saying that all is well in the best of all possible worlds. There are difficulties.
If I may turn to another aspect of the minister's speech in Winnipeg-and I should like to apologize to the committee for concentrating on this-there was one aspect in which I can support him entirely. This is when he says:
The fact that domestic trade takes place in a more familiar and predictable environment, and therefore with less conspicuous effort, should not be interpreted to impute an inferior role to this part of our commerce. On the contrary, the benefits accruing from the exchange of goods and services are equally real, whether achieved in a national or international framework. Canada's voluminous inter-regional trade flows are, in fact, a key pillar of our economic strength and the relative ease with which this movement occurs in no way detracts from, but rather adds to, its value. We would, I am afraid, become painfully aware of the tremendous contribution of inter-regional trade to our economic life were we to experience a serious disruption to the free flow of goods and services, and productive resources generally, across provincial borders. At a time when larger trading units are emerging throughout the world by way of customs unions and free trade areas, it is doubly important that we fully appreciate the value of our unrestricted domestic trade.
I suggest that it should be one of the primary objectives of this chamber of commerce-
I think of all Canadian businessmen and of all governments, if I may interpolate.

-and of its members to resist the efforts that are sometimes made to hamper the free movement of goods within Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, yesterday afternoon I had the oportunity of making a short intervention in the debate, at which time I stressed a similar point. I should like merely to refer hon. members to the remarks I made there and not repeat them. However, I will not back away from them.
Now, may I turn to the national oil policy which was enunciated on February 2, 1961? The minister has told us that production now is about 850,000 barrels a day, and this includes both the domestic market and the export market. At the time the policy was enunciated, if my memory serves me correctly, production was about 630,000 barrels a day. As the minister indicated progress has been made, but not without some difficulty. This was anticipated both by the industry and the government. The attitudes of both were appreciated at the time and it certainly is to the credit of the industry that they have been able to continue this achievement.
The national oil policy was a prediction on a five year basis. We are now approaching the end of 1964, and I should like to hear a good deal more from the minister with regard to oil and gas. The mere fact it is more or less concentrated out in the prairies and in northeastern British Columbia should not detract from its importance. After all, petroleum is the most important mineral in Canada today, in so far as production is concerned. I have here, Mr. Chairman, a publication entitled, "What the mining industry means to Canada", published by the Canadian metal mining association. I received it today. It certainly has some very illuminating statistics at the back, and I commend them to hon. members, showing precisely what the mineral industry means to this country.
It must be remembered that oil and gas are minerals and they form a great part of our mineral production in each year. Now, in 1963, the total mineral production in Canada was valued at $2,976 million. Of this, mineral fuels, which are coal, natural gas, natural gas by-products and crude petroleum made up some $882 million.
It may not be realized that the province of Alberta produces the second largest amount of minerals in the country, on a dollar basis. In fact it produces 21.3 per cent of Canada's mineral production, exceeded only by the province of Ontario which produces 29.4 per cent. I admit this is primarily oil and gas. There is some coal, but when we look at the
Supply-Trade and Commerce production of mineral fuels in western Canada, and what these fuels mean both to our domestic and foreign market then I feel sure the minister will agree that he needs to pay a great deal of attention to them.
The industry has problems. It is operating in a very limited sphere so far as the export of oil is concerned. This is one of the most competitive markets in the world, taking into account both the quantity of world production and the geographical location of our fields in relation to markets in Canada and the United States. I am a lot more confident about the export market for natural gas than I am about oil, because I do not think it will be subject to the same vicissitudes, and I would like an assurance from the minister that a very close watch is being kept on this.
Each time there was a suggestion in the United States press that quotas might be imposed on oil, those now on the ministerial benches used to rise in their places and try to badger the minister's predecessor with respect to the efficacy of the national oil policy. The performance of that policy over the last four years is ample proof it was a wise one. The government of the day followed the wise counsel of the national energy board, and I would like to pay-

I appreciate the courtesy of the committee in allowing me a few more minutes so that I may complete my remarks at this stage. Again with regard to oil and gas, may I point out that almost 72 per cent of our national production is produced in Alberta, 21 per cent in Saskatchewan and almost 5 per cent in B.C. We have a tremendous market for this product and there are pressures to sell more. We have approximately 15,000 producing wells which at present are producing at something like 55 per cent of their economic potential, and we also have the beginning of the development of the Athabasca tar sands in northeastern Alberta. These sands are just on the eve of massive development. Within three or four years we shall be seeing enough oil coming down the pipe line from the tar sands to keep one rather large refinery going, and this is only a mere beginning.
I have seen figures which show that the reserves of oil in the oil sands, sufficient for our requirements both in the export and

domestic market, will last 1,040- years, which gives an indication of the vast potential of the area.
I would like to hear the minister comment on the national economic council, which was introduced with a great fanfare in 1963. There was almost indecent haste to replace the national productivity council with it, and I would remind the committee that the national productivity council was doing good work. Its name was changed to the national economic council and the government replaced its membership to a large degree. Since then there has been a great silence from the council so far as real, hard results are concerned. Listening to the devotees of economic planning who now occupy the government benches, we thought we were going to get the formula for the economic development and salvation of the country, but this seems to be the best kept secret of the year because we have heard nothing of any consequence from the national economic council. At least the government has kept very close counsel in this regard.
It is now five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I shall conclude my remarks for today, but will continue them on another occasion.
