subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, September 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-27, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada-Mr. Brown-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Number of directors.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have grave doubts that the amendment before the committee is in order. The bill asks parliament to enlarge the permissible number of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada from 15 to 20. The amendment asks that three directors out of the 20 be appointed by the governor in council, and this is an innovation that goes far beyond the limits of the original act that incorporated the Bell Tele-

phone Company of Canada and is, I submit, far removed from the scope of an amendment.
I would suggest to the hon. member who moved this amendment, which is so far reaching, that he withdraw it. An amendment of this type should not be brought before parliament except after careful thought, and at an appropriate time. It has been hastily drawn to meet this occasion and could have the opposite consequences to those intended. It would I think be chaotic if members of parliament, or retired members of parliament, or those deserving the favour of the governor in council were to be appointed directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. The governor in council is not a body to appoint directors of a company whose shares are owned wholly by its shareholders.
The mover has, I know, good intentions in his amendment; but I doubt that he or his supporters seriously expect the Canadian parliament to pass it. Its passage would undoubtedly lead to the greatest confusion and to ultimate chaos, turning or prolonging directors' meetings into a fruitless waste of time. Every group asking to be granted a charter might be asked later on, if their company had signal success, to provide for the appointment of directors by the governor in council.
In addition-and I need scarcely mention this-this is an infringement of property rights and the liberty of the subject. It is far different from nationalization, and subsequent compensation to owners and shareholders. It is an invasion of that field of legislation reserved to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces under our constitution. It permits a wholly unwarranted intervention or intrusion by the governor in council into the private affairs of Her Majesty's subjects.
It is particularly significant that this innovation will affect the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, that most Canadian of all companies and a company which operates one of the most efficient telephonic communications systems in the world. The supporters of the amendment have stated that this type of interference by parliament is common in many countries of western Europe. I believe that France was mentioned as a country where some directors were appointed by the government and where the telephone system is partially owned by the state. I would ask any hon. member whenever he goes to France to endeavour to place a long distance telephone call in that country, a country where

the government appoints a percentage of the directors. I would refer hon. members to the issue of Le Figaro Litteraire for the week of August 27 to September 2, 1964, and to read therein the article by Monsieur Francois Nourricier. It took him more than 27 hours to make an urgent telephone call into Paris from a distance of 50 miles away. Merely reading the story would be a salutary experience for many of us. Do the Canadian people want to risk losing the efficient telephonic communications system that it enjoys at the present time in order to experiment with the fanciful provisions of this amendment? I say not, Mr. Chairman; although I want to add that I respect the mover of this amendment and many of the other speakers.
I would remind hon. members that very shortly the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada is to review the financial affairs of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. This is the body that represents the Canadian public in its dealings with the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. Will its functions be aided one iota by a few directors being appointed by the governor in council as a political plum, or honour, if you like, to defeated candidates or even to members of parliament? I would think not. Mr. Chairman, the amendment is unrealistic; it is eccentric and ill-conceived, and will never meet its intended purpose. If it is not wholly out of order, it ought certainly to be defeated in committee.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on this subject. I speak in favour of the amendment which would add public directors to the board of the Bell Telephone Company, and I speak against the original proposal which would add private members to that board. I think it is very timely that we consider that only two weeks ago, as the previous speaker mentioned, the board of transport commissioners virtually called the Bell Telephone Company on the carpet so that it could examine its operations. I think this would be a most untimely period for us to extend the private control of that organization, at least until the board has, as it has announced it will, reviewed the operations of the company.
I need only quote from the statement issued by the board so recently on this subject to explain why many hon. members in different parts of the house are opposed to the extension of the Bell Telephone Company private directors board. I quote from the board's statement:
Private Bills
The periodic studies made by the board's staff and the information supplied by the companies from time to time showed that there had been certain changes in capital investment, revenues, expenses, debt charges, dividend payments and retained earnings of the companies.
This refers to the Bell Telephone Company and to the B.C. Telephone Company. The statement continues:
It would appear to be in the public interest that the board should hold a review by way of public hearings to consider the capital investment, revenues and expenses, debt charges, dividend payments and retained earnings of the company and the permissive level of the company's earnings and the basis on which such permissive level may be authorized for telephone rate purposes.
The board does not intend to inquire into the propriety of existing rates or any revision thereof that may be requested in consequence of the board's finding which will be reviewed later if necessary.
The other telephone company mentioned in the board's statement is the British Columbia Telephone Company, whose profits have risen by more than 100 per cent since 1958. In the case of the Bell Telephone Company, which would add to its directors under the original motion, the total dividends paid increased about 75 per cent in the seven-year period from 1957 to 1964, or from $35.4 million in 1957 to an estimated $61.4 million this year. In other words, the Bell Telephone Company is making over $1 million a week from supplying privately a service that should be, surely, publicly conducted for use and not expressly for profit. This is the basic reason why we in this party feel that if any addition is made to the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company, it should be done by the appointment of public directors, especially at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before I recognize the hon. member for Timiskaming I might mention that when the hon. member for Brantford spoke a short while ago he raised a point of order which I had a chance to consider quickly while the hon. member for New Westminster had the floor. Certainly I feel the same way as the hon. member for Brantford, namely that there is some doubt as to the legality of this amendment, which is unique perhaps in some ways. On the other hand, there has been discussion and debate on it and I believe it would be most unfair to hon. members who wish to take part in the debate if I were to rule on the point of order now. I suggest we continue the debate on the amendment now before the committee.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The remarks of the mover can be concurred in as far as I am concerned because I think

Private Bills
this amendment may have been hasty, and is unique. We in Canada are facing problems which should have been discussed years ago. I agree with the hon. member when he says that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, which serves 400,000 subscribers in Ontario and Quebec, is a worth-while, highly modernized and efficient operation; there is no question about that. We in Canada are very proud of our telephonic communications systems. It is true that in Europe and even in France the situation is such that it would be easier to walk and speak to your party than use the telephone, but I certainly did not say or intend to imply that the telephone communications system in France is operated by government appointed directors, because I do not know whether it is or is not. I do know that many enterprises in France are in that circumstance, but I would not presume to say that their telephone system was.
The board of transport commissioners have, in my opinion, listened to some very odd arguments from the Bell Telephone Company in the past and it is interesting to note they have now decided to review the rates to the subscribers in the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. The board of transport commissioners should have looked at these rates a long time ago.
A chap came into my office the other day who had been doing considerable work in the field of government investment, and it seems governments have involved themselves in communications systems to a large extent. In a country as large as Canada, interlinked as it is with the United States defence system, it is normal that a large system of communications which is absolutely necessary to any type of defence of our nation would be inter-related with other existing communication systems. In most countries I am sure there is a division between private systems in operation, even the monopoly civilian systems, and national defence operations. Because the Bell Telephone Company respect the government and receive co-operation from the board of transport commissioners, they have been an efficient organization, able to supply services required and are able to provide a large amount of money. They are also in a position to take advantage of Canadian and United States defence contracts.
We do not own our own system or even the trans-Canada telephone system, which itself is a pooling of hundreds of telephone systems throughout the country. In 1962 these contracts to which I have referred-I am talk-
ing here of the public tender contracts, not the type given to the Bell which are of a classified nature-amounted to approximately $6,385,000, and in 1963 to $6,869,000 approximately. For the month of August of this year they amounted to $13,277,000 approximately. So that in the first six months of this year they were more than double of the two previous years. That is a factor which must be taken into consideration.
Great emphasis is placed on the fact that this company is a Canadian company, but I do not think it really exists as a company except in the minds of the shareholders. This company is the American telegraph and telephonic system, I am sure. On paper it may be Canadian owned, but there is the same kind of subsidiary in the United States, Western Electric, and in the north there is Northern Electric, a totally owned subsidiary which manufactures parts.
The province of Quebec is interested in doing something about this question. I saw an official the other day who was talking to me about the legality of the action of the Quebec government in taking over the Bell Telephone Company in that province. It is my opinion that if the Quebec government wants to take over Bell's assets in the province of Quebec, they can be expropriated, provided they do not interfere with the federal charter which allows the company to operate on a national basis and is a link between the government, through the board of transport commissioners, and the public.
I think the Liberals had better look at this matter and not hide their heads in the sand. Somebody has to do something about Bell because the rates are far too high. They are almost double what they are in the three prairie provinces which have, in the main, a rural operation. The operation in Ontario and Quebec is mainly an urban one, and in the northern areas of those two provinces other telephone companies operate, similar to those in western Canada. I think the Liberals had better think twice before they reject this amendment. I think the directors of the Bell Telephone at the present time will be happy to accept this kind of control and direction and allow the government to have some small say in its operation, rather than allow the government of the province of Quebec to take over their assets any time they wish to do so by means of expropriation. Many people have said to me: "Let us expropriate the whole of the Bell Telephone". Let us go further and expropriate all the telephone communications systems in Canada, because they are pretty

vicious monopolies. It is impossible to conduct a conversation with a neighbour in a town, to operate a business in a community or to conduct any ordinary type of business without using the monopoly of the telephone company in any given area. In return for that there is some small measure of control by the board of transport commissioners. The board was not set up to look into telephone communications; they were set up to decide the tariffs of railways. They were not meant to decide whether the subscribers rate in Ottawa is $6.50 or $4.25 in northern Ontario, or $3.90 in the prairie provinces. That is not their function, and having talked to some of these officials I know they are not equipped to handle this problem. The public demands some control, and control along the lines suggested in British Columbia. Perhaps a federal charter should not apply and these companies should be forced to obtain provincial charters. If that were the situation I am sure that British Columbia would, by majority decision, expropriate and nationalize the provincial telephone system. I think that will happen in the province of Quebec earlier than the people concerned with this matter think. There is a great deal of interest in the province of Quebec in this possibility, and I can foresee a move being made towards the expropriation of the telephone systems in that province within the next two or three years.
Mr. Chairman, I want to be entirely fair in this matter and must say that it is not only the Bell Telephone Company that creates difficulty for the province of Quebec. I understand there are more than 150 telephone companies operating at the present time in the province of Quebec. Many of them operate very archaic exchanges, and rural systems badly in need of modernization. I suggest that will only be accomplished as the result of the Bell system being expanded in that province. I do not think a provincial system could accomplish this improvement unless it took over the large urban subscriptions, which would of course have an effect on the Bell Telephone Company.
The Bell Telephone Company vice president came to us several weeks ago in Ottawa and said in respect of this increased board of directors that one of the directors to be appointed would probably be a representative from a university. He said one of the directors would be a man now high in the academic field completely divorced from politics and business, but interested in providing the board of directors with some academic experience. He suggested that another appoint-
Private Bills
ment might be made from the industrial sector of the country and this appointee would provide information in respect of industrial aspirations in this field of communications.
Mr. Chairman, I had not heard a government member stand up and say, that if three appointments were to be made by the governor in council, they would be defeated political candidates, until the hon. member made that suggestion today. I had not heard a government member before say that these appointments would be political plums handed out on a patronage basis. I take off my hat to that government member. He has been much more honest and courageous than most members in discussing this very touchy and unique part of our political way of life. He says these appointees will be that type of individual.
Mr. Chairman, I do not believe the hon. member is correct in that suggestion. I do not contemplate such a development. I believe the individuals appointed in this way would be of the calibre and type the government has appointed during the last several years to sit on royal commissions. I think they would be exactly of the type suggested by the vice president of the Bell Telephone Company. One might well be appointed from the economic department of one of our universities. Another appointee might well be an outstanding banker from the Canadian banking association. Perhaps some man off the street would be appointed to represent the consumer. Such an individual could perhaps act as an ombudsman on behalf of the ordinary consumer. I am sure such a man would have experienced a disconnection of his service because he did not pay his bill during a time when he was away on holidays. Every member of this committee I am sure has experienced that situation. The telephone system of today has become so automated the companies really have little or no contact with the average subscriber. Perhaps we need an ombudsman in this field.
The government could appoint outstanding people, as both this government and the former government have done in the past. I am very proud of the fact that our governments in the past have seen fit to appoint men of high calibre to royal commissions and other like bodies. The majority of such appointments have not been made on a political basis, and the men appointed have not been unemployed politicians. The contribution which could be made by three outstanding members on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company could per-

haps stave off the nationalization oi the system. While that may not be the normal way of accomplishing this, I think if it were successful it would be an excellent thing.
I am shocked that most government members are opposed to the type of innovation suggested by the amendment. I think it embodies something that should be attempted. If the sponsor of the bill was instructed to oppose this amendment, then I can only believe he was not fully aware of the situation at the outset. Three new directors, to be appointed by the government are required by this company. Unless we receive a satisfactory reception to this suggestion I think we are better off to kill the bill and let the present board struggle on as it has done in the past.
A young university lad, who is very interested in this matter, asked me why the company needed more directors. I was unable to give him an answer because I honestly do not know. If the A.T.T.C. took over the Bell Telephone Company tomorrow-I am not sure it did not take over that company some years ago-I am sure it would demand representation on the board. The latest telephone system taken over by Bell Telephone Company was a small exchange in Newfoundland, and I am sure that company was not important enough in terms of subscribers, in relation to the systems in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, to warrant the addition of five new directors to the board. I do not think the situation which developed in Kenora in recent days has had the effect of making five additional directors necessary. I have very seldom, if ever, heard of an increase in a board of directors that did not accompany a change in the financial control of the company.
How much is paid to the board of directors? I am sure it does not exceed $50,000. I do not think this company would have any difficulty in paying that extra amount. I understand that something in the neighbourhood of $13 million to $20 million is spent in communications in the field of national defence. That being so, the telephone company does not need individual subscribers. The company is able to profit from communications in respect of restricted fields such as NORAD and the radar systems. This company also provides services in respect of computer operations, telex and other teletype communications systems.
The sponsor of this bill should reconsider his position and his instructions from this company, in refusing to allow the bill to

pass containing the proviso that three of the five members of the board of directors be appointed by the governor in council. This company is desperate. I am sure the sponsor is aware of that fact as I am sure the board of directors is aware of it. It is desperately in need of closer communication with its subscribers. Do you know what the vice president told us, Mr. Chairman? He said: The complaints you make are being investigated and the president of the company has insisted that every complaint come to his attention. Think about that, Mr. Chairman. What is the poor president doing these days other than answering his fan mail from his subscribers? This is not the kind of thing he should be doing. He has a multimillion dollar enterprise to operate and he cannot be listening to the beefs of the subscribers.
The three people who would be appointed as ombudsmen on behalf of the Canadian people could listen to these complaints and I would surmise they would need a very large staff to deal with complaints because you cannot find out anything from the local manager. He really does not know anything. The billing system is based in Montreal. He has no power to make a decision. He does not know what has happened because the computer has not told him. Most of these computers are short on words and long on action. The action is taken long before an explanation can be given and to put a tracer through the computer probably is a very tedious and sterile process when the results are finally returned. When they arrive on the manager's desk I imagine he faces a very confused situation.
If the Liberal government is sincere in saying as they have said in the past that all they want to do is to provide the things the N.D.P. wants to provide but to do so in a more calculated and studious manner after a great deal of thought, they will find that the appointment of ombudsmen to companies that come to parliament for their authorization so that these ombudsmen may make suggestions on behalf of the people of Canada and supervise operations will be a highly acceptable, although novel, method of counteracting the nationalization that will take place in this field if the government fails to act soon. I think that many Quebec members can stand up and say that the taking over of the Quebec section of the Bell Telephone Company has been widely desired in the province of Quebec and is currently under active study by the government of that province. All you have to do is to look at your telephone bill to know why they have been very concerned

about this matter. If the government wants to protect the Bell Telephone Company the action of appointing ombudsmen may provide a safety valve for the subscribers that will be very effective.
In my opinion the governor in council will appoint reasonable, responsible and impartial people to the board of directors to act on behalf of the government of Canada and particularly on behalf of the governor in council and the general public in supervising the operations of the Bell Telephone Company. We must always bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, that this is a national monopoly. We have granted this monopoly to the Bell Telephone Company in a field where even the defence of our nation is involved and one failure might result in a disaster. Let me use an example because we must not be vague about this matter. I had the opportunity-

Mr. Chairman, I would be out of order if I went very far in discussing other telephone and communication companies. If such action were successful in this case I believe that the government would take similar action in the case of all federal companies. We can only do so now in the case of the Bell Telephone Company which has a bill before us, but if this method proves to be satisfactory I see the government asking authorization from parliament to impose the same statutory provision with respect to other companies.

Mr. Chairman, I do not agree with the method proposed this after-20220-547

noon by the hon. member for Timiskaming but I do agree with the objective, and I think that in one of my longer speeches I should say so. I believe this matter could be settled with dispatch if the company would show good, modern social sense and ask the government to nominate three of the 20 directors. They were referred to as ombudsmen but in my view that is not a good term. They could be friends of the public on the board of directors of a company which enjoys a virtual monopoly. I think this would be the better approach.
I am surprised that a great company like Bell has not long since asked the government to nominate three of the 20 directors. This is not a very revolutionary proposal and if Bell would do this it seems to me that this bill would receive more rapid passage through parliament than it is getting. With regard to the last question, I think that any provincially incorporated company, if it has a monopoly, should accept representatives of the government on its board of directors. This is not an unusual thought. Some of these companies are controlled to some extent by public utility boards but it seems to me that there should also be nominees of either provincial or federal governments sitting on their boards as friends of the public. If Bell had displayed a sense of responsibility they would have asked for this and not left it to a committee to make them do it. If they ask for it I have an idea the bill will go through.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak on this Bill No. S-27 which has already been discussed for several weeks.
The purpose of Bill No. S-27 is to allow the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to increase to 20, from 15, the number of directors which they already have or which they are entitled to appoint. This bill was referred to a committee of the house. It came back and we are now discussing an amendment submitted by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the Bell Telephone Company gives good service wherever it is in operation, and I am wondering how the services it gives could be improved by increasing the number of its directors. I truly believe that it could improve its services on all its lines throughout Canada, and I know that it is already attempting to improve them. So, I wonder why vague answers are given to questions asked in the committee, or no answers at all are made, when it is wished to increase the number of directors.

Mr. Chairman, before taking a stand on the amendment now before us there is a point I should like to clear up. On several occasions I asked for the report in French of the committee which considered this bill and once again this afternoon, I was told that there was no French version. On the other hand, for several weeks, the English version has been seen going around, but the French text of this committee report is not available.
Mr. Chairman, I am hard put to study the bill itself or the answers made to the questions. If that report is not presented to us in French, I shall have to move an amendment or a motion to postpone the discussion of the bill until we have the French material we need.
Mr. Chairman, on the amendment before us tonight which was introduced, I think, on September 10, I do not agree with the hon. member for Timiskaming that three of those directors should be appointed by the government.
This amendment is as follows:
The business of the company shall be managed by a board of not less than five nor more than 20 directors, as may from time to time be determined by resolution of the shareholders, and each such director shall be the proprietor of at least ten shares in the capital stock of the company, or such other additional number of shares, not exceeding 40 additional shares, as the shareholders shall by any resolution passed at any annual general meeting, or special general meeting, from time to time determine: and the said board of directors shall be elected and hold office as hereinafter provided; and a majority of the said directors shall be residents of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, in this Bill No. S-27 amendment we have a dose of socialism, a small dose, if you wish, but a dose just the same. I think the government has available legislation giving it power to investigate any Canadian company. There is the Combines Investigation Act enabling the government to take a look at the operations of those companies.
I must admit, however, Mr. Chairman, that this act or these investigations into combines are not too efficient, because they are not always given the priority they should have. The considerable increase in the price of sugar that followed the last general election has not yet been forgotten. We asked for an investigation into combines and we were told that one was under way, that it would take a very long time before we would get its report.
If an effort were made, these inquiries into combines could enlighten us as to the actual situation and we would know whether the company or any other company in

Canada is providing reasonably good service to the Canadian public without obliging them to pay prices that are far too high.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to the amendment as it would enable the government to interfere directly in the company's business or in Canadian institutions.
Mr. Chairman, when the amendment is put to a vote, I shall have to vote against it for the reasons I have just outlined.
I will say no more about this because the debate is now on the amendment only. However, when we come to the various sections of the bill, I shall say what I think of Bill No. S-27.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to participate in the debate, but in view of the various questions raised I want to mention that the discussion which has taken place with respect to Bill No. S-27 proves once more that when private industry -which we favour-becomes a monopoly or a trust, the government must take steps and assert itself.
The amendment now before us concerns the appointment of directors by the government. I am against this proposal for the same reasons my colleague from Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) mentioned a moment ago, since we favour private enterprise.
In my opinion, the Bell Telephone Company operates somewhat like a monopoly. Its rates are too high, especially if compared with those in other provinces.
For instance, in Quebec the monthly rate is $6.46, when the same service is available in Alberta for $3.50. As you can see the Bell Telephone Company really goes too far.
If we had the French version of the proceedings of the committee which considered Bill No. S-27, we would be in a better position to discuss it.
Once more I mention the fact that it is intended to appoint more directors, to whom very high fees will be paid which might entail increased rates.
Mr. Chairman, for all the reasons I mentioned I will vote against the amendment.

I was interested in the statement by the hon. member for Brantford with regard to the French telephone system. I do not recall anyone mentioning the French telephone system. I think if he were to look at the situation in the whole of Europe, he

would find it had very little to do with public or private ownership. It has to do with the lack of subscribers to those systems. It is only in North America that you have these tremendous networks of telephone systems where virtually everyone has a telephone.
Like my colleague from Timiskaming, I was interested in the political plum aspect of the hon. member's discourse, and the rather cynical regard he has for his own government if he assumes they would appoint directors from the ranks of those who usually receive political plums. But, Mr. Chairman, as has been mentioned here, the company has never told us why they want five more directors. I was unable to get this information from the vice president in the course of a long conversation with him. All I got, to be rude about it, was windy nonsense about how they wanted to broaden the base of their directorate; they wanted to bring in people from the various walks of life, the academic and business world. It struck me as rather unconvincing and I am still unable to understand why they come before us for this purpose at this time.
For the life of me I cannot see that the addition of five members is going to make all that difference to them. On the other hand, the proposal made by my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming, that three of these should be appointed by the governor general in council, in the light of speeches a few moments ago, appears to have been received as the first sign of creeping socialism that is going to overwhelm the company.
I said when I spoke first, Mr. Chairman, that my, shall I say, more logical mind would have preferred to see an outright move for the nationalization of this company. I make no bones about that at all. It would appear to me to be the only logical course sensible people would follow, but I am well aware that we are not going to get that at the present time. In the meantime we need some measure of control and observation on behalf of the people of Canada.
I suppose the telephone business, more than any other type of business, is one that has been built up by its subscribers. It is a very different business from most large corporations producing goods, or even services. A telephone company is built-and the history of all our telephone companies is proof of this-by the contributions of its subscribers. The origins of most of the telephone companies in North America were extremely modest, with a very modest amount of capital originally invested and the assets of the 20220-5474

company built up by the contributions of the subscribers-who are actually a captive group, because we cannot take our trade somewhere else if we do not like the telephone company. We have them or we have nothing.
For that reason it seems to me the telephone company is in a peculiar and singular position. It is a necessity for the operation of the modern industrial society. We just could not function without it, and that in itself appears to me to be one overriding reason why the public interest should be protected by the appointment of-and I have more confidence in this government than the hon. member for Brantford-the appointment of responsible people who would undertake their duties seriously, who would realize just why they have been placed in this position and would not consider it merely a plum for a defeated candidate or a reward for party service. Like the hon. member for Timiskaming I think that is a slur on this and previous governments because, while there have been such people appointed, there have also been some very useful appointments of this type.
I notice that there is great concern on the part of some members about the position of shareholders and the rights of shareholders in a telephone company, that they alone should have the right to appoint directors. No one seems to consider the rights of the subscribers or the rights of society as a whole, organized as it is today on a very complex basis and requiring the services of a telephone company in order to operate at all.
My hon. friend from Brantford was citing the horrors of the system in France. I do not know whether the telephone system there is publicly owned or not; I suspect it is but I am not sure. However, right in this country there are publicly owned telephone systems whose operations are in striking contrast to that of this multimillion dollar corporation, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. In all the prairie provinces we have publicly owned telephone companies which operate in much more difficult and expensive areas as regards telephone service than does the Bell company, and in those provinces you will find just as good service as you get from Bell, and the price is less.
I see the hon. member over there shake his head, but I can tell him I have observed when I have taken up a phone in a city like Regina or Saskatoon that I get through just as quickly as I do when I pick up the phone in Ottawa. I have also observed something else, that when I have to use a pay phone in

Private Bills
the province of Saskatchewan I have to deposit only a nickel in the slot, not a dime. If the hon. member is looking for comparisons between public and private enterprise in this field he should perhaps take that particular situation into consideration.
Seriously, Mr. Chairman, I think it is time that the parliament of Canada recognized the developments in the world today, and realized it is ridiculous to continue regarding a telephone company of the dimensions of the Bell company in the same light as we regard other corporate bodies in this country. There are many that should be regarded in the same light. In fact I recall when I was having this interview with the vice president of the Bell company he was very plaintive and he asked, "Why do you pick on us? Why are we the ones who are to be penalized in this manner?"
It was interesting to note he seemed to think that the presence of publicly appointed directors on the board of directors would be a penalty, and that the company would be penalized by that. I assured him I was not anxious to discriminate in any way, that I would be only too glad to propose the same or even more drastic proposals for other corporations in the country, but it was his company's misforture that they had been the first to pop their heads up and enable us to do a little bit of hair cutting on top of their heads. I assured him when others came up I would be there with my shears to do the same with them.
You have got the hon. member for Edmonton West worried.

He has already been sheared. Seriously, Mr. Chairman, I would like to impress on Liberal members of the house who make claims, most of them I think quite sincerely and honestly, that their party is trying to keep abreast of developments in the modern world, that it is a flexible, pragmatic party that takes into account recent developments. This is one of the developments of recent years of which the party should be cognizant and taking action about, namely the development in our society of a privately owned organization which grew from very small beginnings and which now embraces not only this particular company but almost the bulk of the population of Canada in the services it renders.
For that reason I suggest the time is long past when this government, if it is going to do more than pay lip service to its claims,

should be prepared to move into this field in the very modest way we are suggesting. If it had any courage I would suggest it move in much more drastically, but I am not going to suggest more than I think it is capable of doing. I believe members of the Liberal party should screw up their courage to take this minor step toward eventual public control of something which is essential to our society, something which should not be left without public control.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.

You are talking out your own amendment.
Progress reported.
