subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my colleague the hon. member tor Danforth usually speaks for this party on trade matters, but he had a conflict of interest today; he is a member of the flag committee, and I hesitate to say which is the more important task. I shall comment briefly on trade policy and pose some questions to the minister; other members of the party will speak on particular votes of the department.
The hon. member for Edmonton West this afternoon said he would have liked a copy of the minister's statement before the minister read it in the house, so that he might be better prepared to speak on the estimates of the department. I would go a little further than that; I feel that a great deal of information is lacking to opposition members generally when they wish to speak on estimates. We have heard a great deal lately about the need for research assistance for members of parliament, and I think this is shown up very much at a time like this. The only resources we have are our own, and they are limited in some cases. But from reading the departments' reports and keeping files we can amass a certain amount of information on the departments in which we are interested. However, Mr. Chairman, I think the education of M.P.s should go further than that.
Quite a number of years ago I had a short and unsuccessful career in the Department of External Affairs, but there is one thing I do remember from it. When we came to Ottawa as a new group of officers, they did make some effort to educate us. The people from various branches of the government, treasury board, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of National Health and Welfare were brought in to give us lectures. I think we were better people and had a better understanding of the government as a result. No efforts are made in this connection with new members of parliament. I suggest this could be done.
I was reminded of that this afternoon when we received notice that the members of the railway committee and other members interested could meet next week for a meeting on the new railway bill which is coming before the house. I think we could stand a briefing on the operations of a great many departments and we could do our job much better as a result.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some comments on trade policy. I understand that setting trade policy for a country like Canada
Supply-Trade and Commerce is difficult at any time. There is only about one thing on which Canadians generally agree with regard to trade policy; that exports are good and we should have more of them. Aside from that there is very little agreement. We have our producers of primary products who are in favour of exports and low tariffs. We have the manufacturers of this country who by and large are tariff protected; they are not too interested in exports-at least, they have not been until quite recently. Also they are not interested in imports at all. In addition to that we have our regional differences. Some parts of the country are much more interested in exports than others, some are interested in low tariffs and others want tariffs to be maintained.
There are very great regional differences, and I think as a general rule the western and Atlantic provinces are export conscious whereas the central provinces are protectionist conscious. These differences which exist in the Canadian business world are reflected, I think, within every party in this house. At the best of times I think it is very difficult to establish a trade policy which satisfies everyone in the country; but at the present time I believe this is particularly difficult because there are so many uncertainties. The whole question of the United Kingdom and its entry into the European common market is uncertain; the election in the United Kingdom might make some difference to the possible outcome of those negotiations, if they resume. The whole question of the Kennedy round within GATT is uncertain. I suggest that the outcome of the elections in the United States might make some difference to those discussions. The United Nations conference on trade and development was inconclusive and I believe will be resumed; but, again, it is hanging in mid air. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with these uncertainties it is no wonder that no Canadian political party-and I will include my own-has a really coherent trade policy.
Now a word about the Kennedy round. As I understand it, at the present time the various countries are carrying on discussions with the trade groups within their countries to determine which particular items they would like to put forward for tariff reduction. I understand that the government of Canada is carrying on discussions with trade groups in this country at the present time and that they will meet later and sit down to some more bargaining. I think generally most of us want the Kennedy round to be successful. Certainly the Minister of Trade

Supply-Trade and Commerce and Commerce does, and he seems to be placing very great hopes upon these negotiations. If they are successful, I wonder whether the government and its policy-makers are working along the lines that I am going to suggest.
This party has advocated in the past that there should be some kind of trade adjustment act. Presumably If the Kennedy round negotiations are successful and we gain certain concessions in regard to trade with other countries, we will have to make concessions too; and undoubtedly this will affect our manufacturing industries. Some of them may feel hardship. I am wondering whether the policymakers within the government, in the Department of Trade and Commerce or any other department, are making plans for that particular day and have decided what is going to happen to the people who will be affected in the localities which may lose their tariff protection; what may happen to the workers in the industries that may be affected.
It seems to me we should be prepared for that day. If these discussions are successful, we should be prepared for the impact this will have upon Canadian industry. I should think central Canada would be particularly affected. I should like to mention one other point in connection with the Kennedy round: I think they all hope it will be successful, but has the Department of Trade and Commerce given any thought to the consequences if the talks are not successful. I know that the minister would probably prefer not to consider that possibility. However, it does exist. We must take into account for example such questions as the entry into the European common market of Canadian and United States agricultural products. We know there is great resistance in Europe to making concessions in this field. So far as I can determine from my reading, the president of France does not wish the Kennedy round any great success. It seems to me that if he could successfully prevent the type of result the late President Kennedy desired to obtain he would do so, as he prevented British entry into the European common market. It is likely that some of the problems facing the conference will be political as well as economic. As far as that goes, the success of the Kennedy round may be determined by which country has the greatest influence with West Germany-the United States or France. Failure is a possibility for which the minister's planners should be prepared. Are the minister's advisers ready with plans for a Canadian

trade policy if the Kennedy round is not successful? I see the minister nodding his head; perhaps he could say a word about this question later.
I wish to turn now to discuss the resumed conference on the economic development of underdeveloped nations. I was at the United Nations session in 1962 when this question was under discussion. I know the developed countries accepted this conference with great reluctance; it was practically forced on them by the vast majority of the underdeveloped countries represented at the United Nations. I believe the developed countries were overwhelmed by the demands made upon them at that time. I believe there was a feeling that the underdeveloped countries were most unreasonable in their demands. This may have been the case. However, the need is very great. I hope Canada will show considerable sympathy for these countries and do what it can to make the resumed conference a success. This question came to my mind the other day when my hon. friend from New Westminster asked the minister a question about coffee prices under the international coffee agreement. My hon. friend showed some alarm at the increase in coffee prices in Canada and the western world generally. In reply the minister had this to say as reported in Hansard at page 8289, September 22, 1964:
In answer specifically to the question as to whether Canada is satisfied with the operation of the agreement, I would say that this agreement can be improved; and it can be improved, I think, for the benefit of both consumers and producers. I would urge upon my hon. friend who asked this question that it is very much in the interests of all of us, including the consumers of Canada, that there should be reasonable prices for coffee, just as there should be reasonable prices for wheat.
I agree with the minister's sentiments in this regard. One of the problems which underdeveloped countries face is the great fluctuation to which the prices of the commodities they supply are subject. In past years they have often not had sufficient income to carry on the industrial and other types of development desirable. So it is in their interest that commodity prices should remain at a stable and reasonably high level. I cannot argue against that. The same considerations apply in the case of sugar, the price of which has been subject to severe fluctuation in recent years. I suggest to the minister that though there should be stability in the price of commodities supplied by underdeveloped countries the government should consider making some kind of subsidy so that prices do not rise too sharply and cause hardship

to consumers in Canada. I know this is a form of taxation; it is another form of external aid; but it is something which I think is fully justified. I suggest that if the underdeveloped countries generally were to have commodity agreements covering their products it would lead to the stabilization of prices and the elimination of one of the greatest difficulties they face. On the other hand, if the price were so high as to work hardship on Canadian consumers the government should consider providing some relief at home. The two interests could I am sure be balanced.
While we talk a great deal about expanding trade not only with underdeveloped countries but with developed countries which buy a great deal more from Canada than we do from them, there are many inconsistencies in our practices. Japan, though not an underdeveloped country, is a nation which certainly has an unfavourable balance of trade with Canada. Year after year we continue to ask Japan to limit the export of certain commodities to this country particularly in the textile field. Speeches are made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by his colleagues advocated more trade with these countries, while at the same time we are asking them to withhold exports to Canada. The question of textiles is an important one. Is any examination being conducted to find out what the future of the Canadian textile industry would be if there were general tariff cuts? There are presumably answers to these questions. If the tariff were cut by a certain amount, then a certain percentage of the industry in Canada would not survive. If the tariff were cut by a further amount, presumably the section which would not survive would be larger. It seems to me that such a study should be conducted because it does not appear reasonable to ask Japan to withhold exports to Canada at a time when that country is increasing her purchases from us. Not only is Japan increasing commodity purchases here but she is putting up a great deal of capital to develop mines so that the minerals she needs may be available to her. Certainly some group should be giving consideration to the impact of Japanese textiles on the textile industry in the future. I do not think there can continue to be too much protection. I think we shall have to accept more textiles from other countries. If it can be determined that there will be a serious effect on the textile industry, the kind of arrangement I mentioned earlier, a trade adjustment arrangement,
Supply-Trade and Commerce should be made so that those who would lose their jobs would be helped during the transition period.
I suspect that our influence at these trade conferences, GATT conferences and United Nations conferences, is not very great. When the European common market on the one hand, and United States on the other hand, are bargaining I think we have to do the best we can. I am not convinced that Canada has a great influence on the outcome of these negotiations.
I gather from the minister's statements that our trade policy is simply to sell as much as we can. I do not know whether this is a sufficient policy or not. I pose the question, and I wonder if there is very much relationship between the internal monetary and fiscal policies of the government and its external trade policy. It seems to me there are inconsistencies at times. Perhaps we have still to determine what our goals are within the country. Perhaps these will emerge through the work of the economic council of Canada. If we knew where the Canadian economy was going we might know better what we want to see in the external trade field. I pose that as a question, Mr. Chairman, because there seems to be no relationship between the two.
Within the context of the trade policy of "try to sell as much as you can",-and that is the only policy I can observe at the moment-I think during the past year the minister and his department have done a good job. They have apparently successfully continued the selling job initiated by a previous minister of trade and commerce. There seems to be a great deal of activity on the part of the trade commissioners branch in promoting the export of both raw materials and manufactured goods. This export has increased, and I presume it will continue to increase in the future. In looking at the estimates and the budgets for those branches connected with trade promotions I note they have been increased.
We are pleased to see that this government has carried on the policy of the previous government, that of selling to all countries regardless of their international policies, and I am sure there have not been too many complaints on the part of the Canadian public or members in this house regarding sales to China, Russia, Poland and Cuba. We have been selling to any country that wishes to buy our goods.
In connection with Cuba, and I know the trade there is not too large, I should like to

Supply-Trade and Commerce pose this question. Since that country has been cut off from United States markets in respect of a number of manufactured goods, is Canada doing everything it can to gain those markets? I notice that Cuba recently purchased a large number of motor buses from the United Kingdom and has also bought manufactured goods from West Germany. Could we in Canada have obtained any of that trade? The general policy of selling to all countries is a good one, but I think it is dictated by necessity. The trade figures for Canada last year were very good, but what would they have been had we not had fortuitous wheat sales to Russia and China?
The department has carried on a vigorous tourist campaign, and I should like to say a word about that and about the Canadian government travel bureau. I understand some efforts have been made to attract Europeans to Canada as tourists, and more recently to interest Japanese in coming here. I think these efforts are very commendable but I am sure the officials of this department realize that tourists from these countries will always represent a very small percentage of our total tourist trade, and that the greater part of our tourist income is derived from United States tourists.
In looking over the department's report, I note that the Canadian government travel bureau has offices in only four cities, New York, Chicago, San Francisco and Los Angeles. This is one field of operations that might well be extended. There should be offices in cities such as Seattle, Portland, Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Boston and many others. Perhaps the tourist bureau could have more than one officer in many of these cities, because the tourist potential is very great in that country of roughly 200 million people. I think the government must do a double job in this respect. It must attract United States tourists here and convince Canadians to take advantage of the tourist attractions in this country. We are losing the tourism balance in favour of the United States.
The final point with which I wish to deal is one the minister referred to this afternoon when he made reference to relations between the Department of Industry and the Department of Trade and Commerce. He indicated that in his view everything was just fine and that there were no problems. Some of us have the uneasy feeling that there may be a duplication of effort. For example I was checking over the commodity branches of the Department of Trade and Commerce and I noticed they have several divisions including a chemi-


cals division, an appliances division, an engineering and equipment division, various other products divisions, a metals division and textiles division.
In looking at information supplied by the Department of Industry I note there is a chemicals branch, a textiles branch and a wooden products branch. Among the tasks of these branches is the supply of market information to the related industries, and import and export analyses. There is a very strong feeling that the Department of Industry has grown very rapidly and that there is a duplication in that department of the efforts of the Department of Trade and Commerce. There are internal branches in both departments having the same name, and both departments supply import and export information.
The Department of Industry has now been in existence for over a year and perhaps there ought to be an independent analysis of its operations, particularly as they relate to the Department of Trade and Commerce, to make sure there is no duplication and that Parkinson's law is not operating within this new department. There is reason to believe that duplication exists between the two departments and I think this should be avoided if at all possible.
Mr. Chairman, I conclude my remarks by summarizing some of the questions I have posed, and in respect of which I should like to hear the minister comment. Has the government any trade policy other than that of, sell as many goods as we can; and what is the relationship between the internal monetary and fiscal policy of the government and its external trade policy? Is the government carrying out studies to relieve the impact upon certain Canadian manufacturing industries if the Kennedy round of discussions is successful, and are they developing policies which can be used in this country if the Kennedy round of discussion is unsuccessful? I realize that these are questions of some magnitude. However, the minister is very competent, has a large department under his responsibility, and I am sure we will receive some answers from him in this regard.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the statement we heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon could properly be referred to as a bouquet of roses. He seems to think everything that has happened in Canada in so far as his department is concerned is good and that everything has been going along very nicely. He seems to think the

increases this year, as compared to those of last year, or in recent years, are satisfactory. He seems to think that they have been so acceptable there is cause for exuberance in respect of the whole Canadian economy.
At the outset I should like to state that the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics, and received from other sources in this country, bear out to a great degree the extreme optimism obvious in the remarks of the minister. He has indicated that our future outlook in respect of wheat sales is excellent, although those sales may not reach the levels we have enjoyed during the past 12 months. He has indicated that there should be no difficulty in selling this year's crop. He has indicated that our export prospects in respect of lumber and iron ore are favourable, and have been carried on at a reasonably high level during the past few months. The minister has indicated there has been a substantial increase in the export of manufactured goods. We are pleased indeed to hear of these things.
When the minister referred to the matter of our balance of payments he did not say very much. I suspect one of the reasons in that regard is that in this area, in spite of the tremendous increases in certain commodities for export, we are experiencing an even more unfavourable trade balance in so far as our current account is concerned.
I am going to deal with this in a few minutes, Mr. Chairman. There are a number of other things I want to say. I certainly cannot cover the entire operations of the Department of Trade and Commerce but my colleague, the hon. member for Chicoutimi, will be dealing with some other aspects later.
The minister also spoke of new trade patterns that are developing in the world, and said that Canadians generally ought to recognize that we have to modernize our thinking with these things in mind. But he simply left it there. He did not say anything about where these trade patterns were developing, whether they have developed to the point where there is a continuity to them, and in what way they are changed from the old traditional patterns. I should like him to elaborate a little more on these patterns.
The minister also referred to the Department of Industry, its growth and responsibility and some of the things it is charged with doing. I think he also suggested that the Department of Industry is primarily concerned with Canada's internal trade, if I may use that term. I believe he also added that the Department of Industry is primarily con-20220-548
Supply-Trade and Commerce cerned with increasing Canada's productivity while his department is more directly concerned with finding markets for products. That would appear to delineate to some extent the responsibilities of the two departments.
The Department of Industry has been in existence for about a year and I have had occasion to make representations to the department on behalf of some of my constituents, and on behalf of some industries in the province of Alberta. I want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the response by way of action on the part of the Department of Industry as a result of these representations has been less than favourable. In fact, until and unless they begin to show that they are in fact able to do something to promote the expansion of the industrial establishment in Canada we believe that they are not serving any useful purpose at all.
May I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it seems to me that one of the functions of the Department of Industry should be to help Canadian industry to compete with certain imported products, at least in so far as taxation is concerned. The Department of Industry ought to assume the responsibility of seeing that the Department of National Revenue gives at least equal consideration to our own industries in so far as taxes are concerned, as opposed to products being imported from abroad. Some cases have been brought to the attention of the Department of Industry and the Department of National Revenue where there is in fact a much more favourable tax structure for the imported products. I will communicate the names to the department if they would like them although I think they realize that what is involved is bentonite or mud production in Alberta which is very important to the oil industry.
In addition, we have at least one potato dehydrating plant in Alberta that has been shut down for months and months. Repeated appeals have been made to various departments of government, and I might say that the federal government is involved because it is their processing patent, and the fact is, that problems with one of their patents are causing the difficulty. In spite of repeated requests to the federal government they have not shouldered any responsibility in regard to getting this very important plant back into operation by doing something to get around the litigation that is causing it to remain shut.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested this afternoon that in the new tariff negotiations that are going on in Geneva and generally among many of the countries of the world Canada was going to be a tough but not reluctant bargainer. The minister has not indicated up to now whether or not any agreement has been reached between the participating countries in the GATT negotiations in so far as agricultural products are concerned. On May 11 a release was issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce in which the minister is reported as saying:
When detailed negotiations have already been initiated with respect to wheat and other grains, the general rules and procedures for agricultural negotiations have yet to be worked out.
If they have not yet reached the stage where they know the basis upon which they are going to try to negotiate trading arrangements with respect to agricultural products, I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that they have got a lot of work to do yet. We remember that only a few months ago France threatened to pull out of the European economic community unless some arrangement with regard to trade in agricultural products within Europe was reached. We also know that there have been repeated indications in press reports from the United States that the biggest problem in the Kennedy round of negotiations was what they were going to do with agricultural products. I think that Canada has got to pursue this matter. Certainly we need to reach some agreement soon and particularly to lay down the ground rules for how we are going to proceed.
There is another thing that disturbs us about Canada's attitude in relation to the GATT negotiations and that is the way we seem to act with respect to our trade with Japan. The minister says that it is going to have to be a case of give and take and that we could not accept the premise of 50 per cent across the board changes and so on. I agree with all that but in our reluctance so far as Japan is concerned we seem to carry it almost to the point of absurdity. In another press release on May 4 this year the minister had this to say:
As was the case for previous multilateral negotiations in the post-war period, the Kennedy round will be taking place within the framework and under the aegis of the GATT. The GATT is a comprehensive multilateral trade agreement embodying contractual rights and obligations and providing detailed rules and procedures for the conduct of commercial policy. The basic principles of the GATT may be summarized as follows:-


I am only going to read one of them.
(b) Prohibition against quantitative import restrictions except in carefully specified circumstances.
That sounds very good until you apply it to Canada's attitude toward Japanese imports. I believe that we are in fact acting in a wrong way toward Japan. We know that we have had a very favourable balance of trade with Japan over the years. We know that we have a large potential market there for more agricultural products, more iron ore, more timber, for almost all of the commodities that are produced in western Canada for export. But, Mr. Chairman, how can we expect to expand these markets unless we are going to buy something in return? Japan is just as correct in her contention that she must sell to Canada to pay for her imports as is the argument we use with the United States. So, I hope there is going to be a change of attitude on the part of the Canadian government in their dealings with Japan so we do not continue this so-called tough policy in so far as quotas and quantitative import restrictions are concerned.
There is one other very serious problem that I think the minister perhaps brushed over a little bit, if I may use that phrase. It is this matter of our balance of payments. When he was in Los Angeles on May 21 of this year, the minister had this to say:
In the past 12 months, Canada's current account deficit has diminished, thanks to increased commodity exports, to a level of about $500 million a year. But this improvement is partly due to a strengthened communist bloc demand for cereals which is unlikely to hold at recent levels; the basic heavy deficit remains. And what concerns us here, the major source of this deficit continues to be Canada's trade with the United States. For while Canada enjoys a current account surplus of some $640 million a year with the world outside North America, our current deficit with the United States runs to nearly $1.2 billion. About half of this deficit comprises net payments of interest and dividends for which no short term reduction is possible; and most of the remainder is a deficit in merchandise trade.
Well, Mr. Chairman, to get some of the exact figures I turned to the dominion bureau of statistics. As I said, I do not want to throw any cold water on the minister's optimism. In so far as our increased activity in international markets is concerned, the latest statistics we have available come from the dominion bureau of statistics and deal with the second quarter of this year. I will not read all these figures but during the period April to June, between the years 1963 and 1964, our current account had a net deficit increase of $175 million with the United

States. In other words it was $346 million for the second quarter of 1963 and up to $521 million for the second quarter of 1964. The problem is, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the minister's optimism, that if we took away the unusually large shipments of wheat and flour to the U.S.S.R., these figures would look alarming. There is no indication at this time there is going to be a repeat order of that magnitude or indeed of any amount from the U.S.S.R. If all of these other things had remained equal, and leaving out that particular order, these figures would be alarming indeed.
So far as we are concerned, Mr. Chairman, we believe that it might not be possible to embark immediately on a policy that would require the United States to set up a trading policy that would give us the opportunity of selling to them as much as we are obliged to buy from them. However, I do not believe the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Finance ought to be satisfied with anything less than the opportunity to sell in the United States sufficient goods and services to pay not only for our commodity imports from the United States but all of the interest, dividends and other commitments as well.
Now, it is all very well to say that we welcome foreign investment. It is all very well to say that this helps develop the country. But what has been happening over the years has been that we have been selling out more and more of our industrial establishment to pay for this. As I said, we believe that we ought to have an understanding with the United States that, on the one hand we be allowed to sell sufficient goods and services to the United States so that we balance, on the other hand, with the interest, dividends and cost of imports so far as Canada is concerned. There is only one conclusion that can come from carrying on the way we have been. If we do not have an opportunity to pay for the investments, whether it is money on loan, an investment in common stock or capital investment, the only other alternative is to sell out the ownership of our industrial establishment. In other words, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that our aggregate obligations to the United States should be matched by the opportunity to sell the United States raw materials or manufactured goods, because I do not believe any Canadian is very happy over the prospect of selling out our industrial establishment to the tune of several hundreds of millions of dollars each year.
20220-548i
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I want to say a word or two now about this matter of wheat and flour. I join with the minister in his optimism respecting what has happened during the past 12 months. Even at the risk of repeating myself I should like to say I do not want to throw any cold water on the achievements in so far as these markets are concerned. I do not want to take anything away from this very good record. However, I should like to say to the minister the picture is not quite as bright as he indicated, particularly when we consider our position in relation to some other countries. For example, I have before me a publication from the Searle Grain Company Limited, dated June 25, 1964, and it gives an indication of what the United States has been doing during the past few months in so far as the export of grain is concerned. I quote:
For some time now, we may have tended to minimize U.S. competition by suggesting that it largely represented "give-aways" against which we in Canada could not compete. It will be noted that this is no longer true to the same extent. Over-all commercial sales by the U.S.A. this year to date are almost three times what they were during the corresponding period last year, while non-commercial or "special program" sales are only slightly higher, by less than 10 per cent.
Noted particularly should be the gain in U.S. wheat sales to such countries as United Kingdom...
During the period about which I am speaking, between 1963 and 1964, the increase in wheat sales through commercial channels from the United States to the United Kingdom was 495 per cent; to Japan it was up by 115 per cent; to the Netherlands, up 119 per cent: to Belgium, up 373 per cent; to West Germany, up 54 per cent. These are not giveaway programs, Mr. Chairman, these are sales of wheat that are going through commercial channels and for which these countries are paying.
When you look at the figures of United States regular commercial wheat sales they make our own sales of wheat and flour look a little less attractive. Again, I do not want to take anything away from the minister's achievements, but another point is that our over-all figures have not gone up as rapidly as those of the United States. Included in our expanded exports are the deals with the U.S.S.R. which we will not be able to repeat, or that at least apparently we will not be able to repeat.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, again I voice the anxiety that we in this party have expressed on a number of times in the past. The tremendous sales we made to China and Russia are all very well, but will they take away from our efforts to expand our regular

Supply-Trade and Commerce commercial markets? If all our expansion of wheat sales are channelled into China and Russia and then are suddenly cut off, where does that leave us in relation to other friendly nations with which we should be expanding our wheat sales?
The indications of the past 12 months have shown that other nations are expanding in our traditional markets, and this is something of which many Canadian farmers are not aware. I want to repeat that I am not against the selling of wheat to communist countries, but let us not reduce our efforts to the point where other countries take over our traditional markets.
Our sales of wheat and flour to Japan have increased substantially, but we should look at what some other countries have been doing. I quote again from the Searle Grain Company report, this time from the issue of July 8:
While Canadian spring wheat continues to be the principle ingredient in Japanese bread, U.S. hard winter is gaining wider acceptance, accounting for almost half the total U.S. wheat sales to Japan last year. In 1960, before U.S. promotion began to emphasize hard winters, exports of this wheat type were insignificant.
Here again we see some of the promotional and salesmanship efforts of the United States to gain part of our traditional markets, and I hope we will not relax our efforts to build up these markets.
Turning to the production of flour, I want to compliment the minister and the government for the action they took approximately a year ago when between 29 million and 30 million bushels of the Russian wheat order were delivered in the form of flour. This was one of the greatest boosts the Canadian flour milling industry had since the end of the second world war. A year ago approximately 50 per cent of the Canadian flour milling industry was shut down, and the amount of the wheat order delivered in the form of flour was approximately the same as the total unused capacity of the industry, and its ability to turn it out during that period of time. The industry appreciated that, but at the end of July the order was fulfilled. The milling had all been done and all the ships had been loaded.
Where do you go from here? Mills are again shut down. At this point it is not particularly distressing because some maintenance work had to be carried out in the mills. A lot of back holiday time was due to employees, and I expect some of the mills have been working to restore inventories in Canada to a reasonable level. However, we


need some statement from the minister on future prospects for flour sales.
On a number of occasions the minister has told us he has had meetings with spokesmen for the flour milling industry. Each time we have asked him about these meetings his answer has been the same, that they were discussing the matter and were hoping to announce something soon. So far I have not seen any positive announcement which would indicate there will be any expansion of flour orders.
For years Canada has enjoyed a good flour market in Africa and southeast Asia, but now the United States with its giveaway programs and foreign aid, has moved in and dried up many of Canada's traditional markets for flour. Something ought to be done by our government to convince the United States that the subsidies it is paying for exporting flour, even into commercial markets, are unfair and unjust so far as its large neighbour to the north is concerned. It is difficult for our mills to compete with the United States treasury, and in closing my remarks I would impress upon the minister that we would like some positive statement regarding prospects for the Canadian flour milling industry.
We would also like the minister to make a statement on the government's policy concerning our balance of payments with the United States. It should impress upon the United States authorities that we will not be satisfied unless we are allowed to export in commodity trade to them sufficient goods so that we can pay, not only for our imports from the United States, but also for our other non-commodity obligations.
I have in my hand a copy of the statement made by the minister in the House of Commons on June 17 when he announced the initial price for grain in western Canada. In that statement he said:
I wish to inform the house that initial payments for the basic grades of western wheat, oats and barley delivered during the 1964-65 crop year will be at the same level as the present crop year.
I mention this because the minister is responsible to parliament for the Canadian wheat board, and I ask why it was that not until well in September were many farmers paid for the deliveries they made to their local elevators in August? If the government informed the wheat board on June 17 of what the initial payments were to be, why was it that the board could not authorize the elevator agents to issue the grain payment tickets until September? I know of points
865S

in western Canada where grain tickets were not released until the first week in September. This means that grain had been hauled to the elevators and was in storage tor five weeks before the elevator agents were authorized to pay for it.
In some cases they accepted advances under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, but to me this was a silly procedure because in the middle of June the government had announced what the price would be. However, that information apparently was not communicated to the agents until September. We do not understand the reason for this. It is something which happened previously and I would like the minister to tell us why it is necessary to hold up these payments.
The minister has painted a very rosy picture of Canada's prosperity and of significant increases in trade with most nations of the world. We hope that some consideration will be given to the problem of balance of payments and to building up some of the traditional markets we rely upon for wheat exports and the export of other commodities, markets such as Japan which is interested in buying increased quantities from us.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to address a few comments to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) during consideration of his estimates, but before doing so I am going to read a few liries from the speech he made on September 28 last at the 35th annual congress of the Canadian chamber of commerce in Winnipeg.
I will then draw a comparison between what he said in his speech and the figures he is submitting to the house, as I have noticed that the minister was very enthusiastic when he made his speech and was particularly proud of export figures for the year. We are as pleased as he is, for we can see that he is giving special importance to exports in general and to wheat exports, a subject I shall not deal with here, since the member who spoke before me covered the matter very thoroughly. And it was only proper that he should do so, because the prairie people always know how to defend their special product-wheat-and we cannot hold that against them.
Mr. Chairman, I will quote some paragraphs from the speech which the minister delivered on September 28:
To link the prosperity of Canada with its flourishing exportations has become a platitude. In fact, it is now evident that the increase in the gross national product in 1964 will be higher than the
Supply-Trade and Commerce 7 per cent which it almost reached last year, which shows an increase in the rate of our development.
The increase in our exports greatly contributed to this sustained expansion. For the period 1960 to 1963, Canada's merchandise exports increased by 30 per cent; to date, the exportations in 1964 increased by 23 per cent as compared with 1963.
If the exceptional wheat sales are not taken into account-
This is exactly the point which I want to forget this evening, and the minister does not take it into account, because he speaks about merchandise exports.
-exports are up by 17 per cent.
A little further, the minister says:
However, according to available figures up to this day, this improvement of our external accounts was not maintained this year. The accelerated growth in the Canadian economy accompanied by sharply expanded capital expenditures has entailed a new upsurge in import demands. The merchandise imports-
Mr. Chairman, I draw the attention of the house to these words:
So far in 1964, merchandise imports are up by 17 per cent over 1963, and payments for non-merchandise items are also up sharply.
Mr. Chairman, after reading those few lines, a question naturally comes to my mind. Who derived more benefit from these exports? To whom does the importation of manufactured goods, often made out of our exports of raw materials, cost more?
Even though we boast about being an exporting country, if foreign investors-since foreign capital is used to develop our natural resources-benefit from our exports to an extent of 80 per cent, Canadians must be satisfied with crumbs.
On the other hand, if the increase in our imports is equal to the volume of our exports for 1963-64, as suggested by the minister, and taking into account that Canadians are paying for 80 per cent of those imports, it means that the imbalance between our exports and our imports results in a double loss for the Canadian people in general.
Indeed, as we export mainly raw materials, thus disposing of our natural resources at a dizzy rate, we only guarantee crumbs for our people.
On the other hand, we import at an accelerated rate finished products which could advantageously come out of Canadian factories, thus avoiding the drain on Canadian capital necessary to the upsurge of our economy.
What is the purpose of building our economy by always reinforcing the top in such a way that, one day, the foundations will suddenly collapse?

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Is it not wiser for a responsible businessman to satisfy the customers who are close at hand before trying to get the business of distant communities?
If, after his first ventures, the merchant finds himself with a surplus, it is normal for him to try to expand his operations. The same holds true for our trade relations. To try to make an exception to the general rule is to court deficits and bankruptcy. We are ridden with debts and deficits at present. The worst part of it is that we refuse to admit that we have made a mistake; indeed, so-called brilliant people claim that the countries and provinces which are getting into debt are those which are run by truly able administrators. We must come to our senses and realize that an economy has to be built from the bottom up and not from top to bottom.
At the risk of being at variance with our great socialistically minded economists, I will again state those great principles. Being the bridge between production and consumption, trade must not destroy one to protect the other. On the other hand, if the welfare of the individual is the end product of any economic system, one must get down to the level of the individual to assess the damage caused by an economy which fails to accomplish its purpose because one of its elements, trade, is not directed towards the achievement of the primary goal.
Is our trade not a striking illustration of the famous trade in ivory, which was practiced in African countries, when foreigners destroyed everything on that continent, giving the poor natives but a few pennies while removing all the wealth from their country.
In order to increase exports mostly carried on by foreigners, we are bleeding our country. For instance, in order to increase our pulp and paper exports, we let foreign companies ruin our forests without compelling them to renew them.
, Why not compel those companies to replant a tree, under the pretext that this will give $6 a cord to the lumberjack, while this same cord of wood will net from $140 to $150 to that company to which all possible guarantees have been granted?
I am not opposed to lumber exports, but I believe they should be rational or-so our socialists may better understand-planned.
I say that trade should first serve regional interests, through the creation of manufacturing industries, for the requirements of the district, the province and the country. After
IMr. Gauthier. 1
this first stage foreign countries may benefit from our surpluses.
But, for God's sake, let us stop giving our raw materials at ridiculous prices and import them afterwards as finished products at astronomical prices.
That is the main reason for our adverse trade balance which reached the terrifying amount of $1,500 million in 1959 and which we reduced to $500 million in 1963, by allowing this national suicide of our natural resources.
If we keep that pace, Mr. Chairman, we will be able to pride ourselves of having sold out the wealth of our children.
Fortunately, the minister gives us a gleam of hope in indicating that he shall turn to domestic trade.
In fact if we take a look at page 6 of the report of his conference, we read:
Exports are important, but let us not forget that about four fifths of our national product is disposed of on the domestic market and that a very large share of that percentage is represented by the interprovincial flow of goods and services.
There is at least one story that the minister leaves us as a consolation and I hope wholeheartedly that it will not be merely a consolation but that he will make it a policy.
If the minister really wants to work in the way he indicated in his conference, he must absolutely turn to primary industry. And we shall succeed in that field by developing our domestic trade, the nearest to us and also the most important.
A man is only as free as he is self-supporting. The same applies to a nation. Our trading ideal must be a self-supporting Canada. To hit such a target, there is only one way: the development of our manufacturing industries.
Let us take a look at countries where planning was made from the bottom up, that is where private industry was the ward of the nation: we realize with great pleasure that such countries are not plagued with unemployment.
In Canada, where we have all the opportunities, we are obliged to import too many essential products because of irresponsible governments which were unable or unwilling to help our fellow citizens in their efforts.
That is a very serious failing. And when those governments took pleasure in bombarding the few Canadian industries that had had the courage to establish themselves with every type of tax, to the point of wiping them out, I cannot find words strong enough to qualify their actions.

Today taxes on Canadian industry and Canadian capital remain the public enemy No. 1 of our industrial and commercial development. Canadian capital is now being called up through all the propaganda media -it being added that this is how we can become masters in our own house. These calls make me think of moose hunters who imitate the beast's call the better to get it into range.
You may be sure that as soon as the new capital is on the market the tax inspectors and collectors will be on the watch. And those who are too daring had better watch out.
Do you really believe there is lack of capital in Quebec for instance? I do not. On the contrary, there are still well-lined stockings to be found in Quebec, but they are buried in the ground to avoid taxation. Canadians are not asking for very much in return for allowing the country to take advantage of the millions of dollars that are hidden away. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) only has to assure them that they will be granted the same exemptions as those granted foreign capital in their own country.
Do you really believe that Canadian interests are better served by dealing so strictly with Canadian capital? Do you believe you are helping Canadian trade to develop by submitting small and medium industry belonging to Canadians to unbearable fiscal obligations? I believe that so far you have achieved exactly the opposite results.
Eliminate taxes on all Canadian capital for a few years. Grant some tax exemptions not only to the industries which dare to settle in a depressed area, but to any new industry, in order to enable them to survive the difficult first years.
In a few years you will be glad for having permitted new industries to make a new contribution to our trade.
The government is not to be given too much credit for the increase in our raw materials exports, since that increase is the result of a further ransacking of our natural resources to the benefit of foreign countries.
If, after supplying 90 per cent of the domestic market, the government should announce a high percentage of finished products in our exports, then it would deserve our congratulations.
Again, the time of long speeches should be over and the government should take immediate action at the regional level, through efficient and well planned marketing. Guar-
Supply-Trade and Commerce anteed markets is the key to the survival of our industries.
Let us consider agriculture. What made western Canada prosperous as it is today? The marketing of their products. When western farmers did not have those guaranteed markets, they were poorer than our Quebec farmers.
We need markets for our dairy products and their by-products. Markets for all our market-gardening industry, for our apples, honey, maple syrup, potatoes and all our fruits, wild as well as cultivated.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce travels around the world selling wheat, as if wheat is the only thing Canada produces. And when we talk "consumer goods", again we talk about wheat. This one-track-minded-ness must cease; let us start looking upon the whole country as a possible trade zone, and not only upon one area of the country.
They say: We are going to double our efforts with regard to our domestic trade. There has been enough talking; it is high time we started finding the markets the eastern producers have been waiting for.
The minister has told us that he will oppose the economic balkanizing of Canada. I wonder if we have not been doing exactly the contrary for the last 25 years.
Let us first have trade equity within Canada; we can then be proud of a flourishing foreign trade, after having achieved the real goal of any sound economic system, the supplying of the domestic market, for the "better-being" of every individual.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I notice the minister looking my way and I assure him that I will be very brief. I should like to make one or two comments in respect of the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. I do not see him in the house at this time, but he suggested that it would be a good idea for members of parliament to attend classes and receive lectures from the ministers. This is a novel suggestion in my opinion because I think members of parliament do not generally want to listen to lectures on the part of ministers, but rather deliver lectures to ministers.
Mr. Chairman, I intend to confine my remarks to that very limited item in these estimates in connection with tariffs on automobile parts and the related agreement. If I understand the situation correctly, under a proposed agreement, Canada would allow the import of certain parts made in the United

Supply-Trade and Commerce States, provided Canada could export an equivalent amount of parts. I understand some of the manufacturers of United States automobile parts are not happy about this arrangement and are urging the government not to put tariffs on our exports because that would, in the vernacular, queer the whole deal.
Mr. Chairman, I think the suggestion proposed in respect of this automobile parts agreement represents a very important part of our export policy, and I hope to see this type of thing adopted as trade principle. I certainly urge the minister to do everything possible to keep this agreement in effect.
In view of certain objections on the part of United States automobile parts manufacturers toward this agreement, will it not be possible to include, so far as Canada is concerned, not only car parts but parts for farm tractors, motorcycles and other pieces of machinery of this type? I suggest this machinery all falls within the same or a similar category.
As one hon. member opposite has stated, everything should be done to continue these transactions, because it is possible for this country to maintain a balance of trade, yet not really use to capacity our own resources. One must consider that we sell $1,700 million of aluminum, but that amount actually represents electric power, transportation and other services. Does it mean on the other hand that we can import $1,700 million of automobile and farm machinery parts? The same situation is true in respect of the export of gas and other raw materials, or a combination of them.
We will eventually have to propose to other nations with which we hope to carry on trade that we import no more than we export, or we export as much as we import. I am sure if every nation followed this practice the balance of trade would depend on quality rather than quantity, and the country which could produce an article better and more efficiently would be the country which would have a better import-export balance. I have no doubt at all that here in Canada we could develop an aircraft industry second to none in the world. We have the raw materials, cheap power and the know-how, and there is no reason at all why we should not become the world's most efficient producers of aircraft. This is a product in respect of which there is no transportation costs because an aircraft can be delivered to any place in the world.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest the outcome of the trade situation developing will depend upon

agreements such as the one I have envisaged. As an example, if I manufactured air conditioning equipment, and I might say that I have, and I exported $1,000 worth, I should receive a permit to import $1,000 worth of equipment of the same or a similar category. If I do not use that permit, rather than the government taking the tariff charges as a penalty I should be able to sell the permit on the open market. I might then receive 18 cents, 20 cents, or 30 cents on the dollar, which would help me balance my export-import situation, and would at the same time do something for the tariff position. I suggest the situation would balance out automatically and assist in providing a balance of employment and a balance in terms of supply and demand. We need to have a balance of export and import trade in accordance with skills, man-hours of skills, but not necessarily dollars because dollars are not a true criterion. I said I was going to be brief. I would urge the minister to do whatever he can with American manufacturers and the American government in this very important field, so that we may continue this agreement with the United States and be able to expand it to other categories of products from time to time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words tonight with respect to trade and commerce. I was interested, and I am sure many other hon. members were, in the statement of the minister this afternoon. I am also sure that a great many will be interested in reading Hansard tomorrow in order that they may get the full portent of his complete statement including, of course, some of the statistics he quoted. He delivered his speech very rapidly. There were a number of things I should have liked to write down but that was impossible and I am sure many other members also found it impossible.
However, Mr. Chairman, I believe the first sentence the minister uttered in his report to the house this afternoon proved the falsity of the Liberal campaign charges that the Canadian economy was stagnant. The committee will recall that in March and April of 1963 many such statements were made. One of the Grit slogans of that time was: "Let's get the economy rolling again". But the minister said this afternoon and also in his speech recently at Winnipeg, I believe, that the advance in the economy commenced some four years ago. That would place it in 1960. I should like to compliment the minister on his honesty. I think what he said is

a wonderful tribute to the former minister of trade and commerce and it is also a tribute to the former minister of agriculture.
I should have liked to speak very briefly this evening on a subject which I am afraid might be forbidden. I believe the operation has been transferred from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of Industry. I was going to speak rather briefly on the subject of the plight of the small businessmen and it is unfortunate I will not be able to do so, because they are having great difficulty. I believe this matter now comes under the Department of Industry. I should like to have some clarification on that point because there is so much duplication and it is difficult sometimes for a new member to know exactly what department is responsible for some of these matters. This causes a great deal of confusion particularly in the minds of the newer members.
I should also like to mention at this time that while the minister has been particularly optimistic, which is perhaps a very good thing, there have been many impediments thrown in his path, one in particular which I will mention. I refer, of course, to the 11 per cent tax on production machinery. Naturally this increases prices and when you increase prices there is a tendency toward pricing yourself out of certain markets. But in spite of that we must say that the minister's department has certainly made progress. This is what we are all looking for, of course, because I think most members of the house are first of all Canadians and, second, party supporters.
I should like to say a word or two tonight about the imbalance of our export-import trade. In 1963, for example, our trade with the United States amounted to about $8.41 billion. This represented roughly 62 per cent of our total trade. I am just wondering whether as a trading nation we are on a very sound footing when we do approximately twice as much business with the United States as we do with the rest of the world. In 1963 our purchases from the United States amounted to over $500 million more than the amount of our sales to that country. This is made somewhat more easy to take in view of our favourable trade balance, in some cases very favourable, with such countries as the Soviet union, Japan, China, West Germany and, of course, Great Britain. But I think this is a time when we should be particularly objective in our thinking because sooner or later these countries where we enjoy these more favourable trade balances
Supply-Trade and Commerce are going to demand a greater amount of our import business, and when they do we are not going to be in any position to turn a deaf ear to them if we hope to continue to enjoy the amount of business we do with them at the present time.
The minister referred to certain statistics this afternoon and I hope I have it right, that exports to the United States are up 11 per cent this year and exports to Great Britain are up 21 per cent. Mind you, on the surface this looks pretty good but let us look at the situation from another angle. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1964 we had an increase of something like 6 per cent, and while this looks good it is not so reasonable when you consider that our general export business increase was something like 11 per cent.
Why do we export mainly only to the larger countries? I think this is something to which we should give a great deal of consideration. Why should we not look a little bit farther into the future? This afternoon we heard about what has happened in the past, but what about tomorrow and next year? What is our policy? What is the matter with our vision? Why is the bulk of our trade done with the United States, Great Britain, France and Germany?

Because they are the richest
countries.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
speechtext:
In 1963, for instance, we did twice as much business with France as we did with the entire Middle East. Our sales to Japan were three times our sales to all of Africa. In the whole of South America our sales were less than those to West Germany. What is the matter with our sales efforts? Some years ago I was quite interested in sales work. I had a staff of some 200 salesmen working under me and our market was the entire Dominion of Canada. We used to sit down from time to time, assess the situation, go over the whole area, mark out those areas of the territory that we covered and try to improve our sales efforts in every area.
It is our business to develop trade throughout the entire world and, knowing the Minister of Trade and Commerce as I do, I would imagine that he must be sitting down and assessing the whole picture with a view to a rapid expansion of our trade policies. There used to be an old slogan we referred to in our sales work and I am sure it would come in handy today. We used to say: "First you plan your work and then you work your plan".

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The optimism shown by the minister is a wonderful thing but you cannot allow that to go too far because the next step could possibly be apathy and maybe indifference. At some time we might find ourselves in the position of the proverbial ostrich which placed its head in the sand. I think we should pull our head out and take a very good look around to see what there is in the way of export markets where we could expand.
To take a look at the South American continent, last year we purchased from Brazil approximately $31 million worth of merchandise. However, we only sold them about $29 million worth of goods. Here is a country conveniently located, with a rapidly growing population now of over 75 million people. Surely this is a convenient market that should be explored to the nth degree. I should like to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the accumulation of all these things could have a profound effect on balancing our budget and also in assisting us in attaining a balance of import-export trade.
There are a couple of questions I should like to leave with the minister, and I am sure he will provide the answers. First I should like to ask, what are the plans for the future? What is to be our trade policy? Second I should like to ask about the budget of Expo '67, which was mentioned in the house this afternoon. We have heard many other names for it, but I rather like this name. I should like to know what is the total cost to date to Canada of the 1967 fair which has been referred to as Expo '67.
I should like an answer to that. There are two more questions I should like to ask in connection with this exposition. What is the anticipated total cost of our 1967 world fair, that is for the entire operation? What disposition will be made of the permanent buildings. These were paid for with the taxpayers' money. What part of that money will be recaptured, and how is it to be decided? I think the public is entitled to the answer.
I should like to place it rather firmly on the record, Mr. Chairman, that I am wholeheartedly in favour of this centennial world fair or Expo '67 as you may wish to name it. I think this is a good location. When we have the Canadian national exhibition in Toronto, it would seem only right that we should have the other exhibition in the largest city in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having been engaged in international trade for several years, I am of course still very interested in problems arising out of international exchange of goods and services.
This afternoon, I listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) with the same attention as that with which I follow his activities. I think the English proverb "The right man in the right place" applies very well to him. I recognize that he is a great negotiator; I must pay this tribute to him. I should also say that his parliamentary secretary is a great help to him.
Furthermore, I must add that he has the support of a remarkable team of men of great merit, stationed in strategic posts throughout the world, to conduct business on behalf of Canada. I see in the galleries several officials who second his efforts here in Ottawa. As a matter of fact, I remember a few I met in Brazil, for instance, and I could name Mr. Holton, in Sao Paulo, and Mr. Cole, in Brasilia, remarkable polyglots very anxious to expand our trade with South America.
At this stage, I should like to stress the importance for our representatives abroad to speak French and English perfectly, because those are two great international languages understood throughout the world.
It is especially during this trip that I became deeply convinced that the exchange system was definitely defective.
Mention was made over there of operagoes paralelas, parallel operations, that is, goods

exchanged against the mutual acceptance of each currency, according to a predetermined equivalence.
So when I came back it occurred to me to introduce Bill No. C-24, whose purpose was to permit the Bank of Canada to keep in its foreign reserves up to $500 million in unconvertible exchange, in order to greatly increase our external trade.
Then, an hon. member opposite said that to reach that goal, the Bank of Canada would have to sell $500 million of Canadian securities. What a monumental joke. One has to be unaware of banking operations to make such a suggestion.
That is why I should like to quote what Mr. James H. Gallager, of Toronto, wrote to me recently.

The present world monetary system Is not the type of system which promotes prosperity in all nations... All nations should exercise control of credit and currency within their own boundaries. A world monetary system does not require financial contributions from 102 member nations to operate efficiently. All that is required is for a world bank to have currency which would be used and accepted by 102 member nations to make up deficits in trading transactions between nations. Within nations themselves, the central banks of nations can balance potential consumption of goods and services with potential production of goods and services within nations.

In my opinion, this Canadian citizen in Toronto is perfectly right.
I suppose that the minister attended the meeting of the international monetary fund when he went to Japan recently.
Perhaps he had an opportunity to hear Mr. Valery Giscard d'Estaing, the French minister of finance, propose an improvement of the international payments system by the abolition of the gold exchange standard because that is the basic cause preventing the exchange of products between countries.
Incidentally, I should like to point out that Mr. Giscard d'Estaing is recognized as one of the best financial experts in the world. In fact, in its issue of September 25, 1964, Time Magazine published an article praising him highly and stated that because of his financial administration, France had a balanced budget for the first time in 34 years.
Mr. Chairman, we must open our doors to friendly countries, because Canada is a country of abundance, except for the 3,800,000 Canadians living in poverty, and we can trade with all those nations to exchange our agricultural and industrial products, and even our
Supply-Trade and Commerce services. In that regard, I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce should use all his influence to promote a Canadian foreign trade bank, on the model of the United States export-import bank, and of the French bank of foreign trade.
A Canadian foreign bank could look after credit operations concerning the financing of foreign trade, including the documentary credit, because Canada is a trading country and all banking facilities must be made available for the exchange of our products by some institution of the federal government, to which belong the monetary authority and power.
I feel that a serious mistake was made in 1961 when the government allowed chartered banks to acquire the Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited, a company set up by a special act of parliament in June 1959, and whose main purpose was to help finance exports guaranteed by the Export Credit Insurance Corporation, a state corporation.
Through this finance company banks make further loans (bank or scrip money) which are also guaranteed by the taxes of the Canadian people. This is an abnormal combination because it is not normal that Canadian taxpayers should take all the risks instead of commercial banks.
At this point I should like to say a few words about the textile industry which faces tremendous competition because this industry employs a great number of Canadian workers and must be protected at all costs.
We know that Japan has taken a rather firm stand, but we must always keep in mind that we must protect the industries with a large labour force as it is an essential step to eliminate unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, these are a few suggestions I wanted to make to the government so as to increase our trade, because our economy is too vulnerable, as a result of the concentration of the majority of our exports to a few countries only.

Business of the House
on generalities I may have the opportunity to adjourn the debate, then study his speech and comment on it at the next opportunity.
All of us who study this department are impressed by its complexity and by the difficulties an ordinary member experiences in trying to assess a department of this size and to assess the work of the minister. One of the problems we have is a serious lack of a good statistics gathering service. I am of course thinking of the d.b.s. upon which all of us rely. The information we are able to collect is that the statistics gathering agencies of the government are starved for personnel in many areas. We hope this is wrong, but I would be interested in the minister advising the committee on the recruitment requests that have been made by the various agencies of the d.b.s., on how many people they have recruited for additions to their staff, on how many of these have been recommended by the minister and, more importantly, on how many of them have been turned down by treasury board.
It is my understanding that these agencies have requested additional staff in very considerable number, that the minister has concurred in this, but that it has been rejected by the treasury board. If this is so it is a sad state of affairs, because I do not know how the minister and, more importantly, how individual members of parliament will be able to judge some problems if they do not have the necessary statistical information available.
For example, I understand a very small degree of good planning is taking place in some areas and that the government has discontinued real studies on input and output tables with any great degree of regularity. Without this kind of economic research it is hard to know how we can do any real effective planning.
I would like to know the size of the economic research staffs. Again it is my impression they are pretty thin in numbers, and if we are to do a fair amount of planning an increase of some 200 per cent to 300 per cent is necessary in the staffs of many of our research units. If we are going to do effective planning we have to have this help available. Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock. Progress reported.
