maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-LA MACAZA, QUE.- TREATMENT OF PEACE DEMONSTRATORS BY R.C.A.F. POLICE
NATIONAL DEFENCE-LA MACAZA, QUE.- TREATMENT OF PEACE DEMONSTRATORS BY R.C.A.F. POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for almost three weeks I have been asking the government to investigate a disturbance which took place at La Macaza,
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Quebec, on September 9 and 10, at which time it was alleged that there was ill treatment of certain persons who participated in a peace demonstration. This afternoon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) gave the house a report. In my opinion that report was a travesty. In the first place, it was not an independent investigation; it was an investigation based entirely on reports from the minister's officials. I would hardly expect a report to be objective that was made by men who are asked to give their opinion on their own competency or the competency of their subordinates.
The minister endeavoured to dismiss the whole matter by quoting from a press dispatch. If it was the same one that I saw, it was a dispatch of September 10 in the Globe and Mail which said that the demonstrators were pleased with the results and that they considered the whole demonstration a successful action.
If the minister is that good at reading press reports he might also have read some of the other press reports. He might have read the press report of September 16, which gave the account of a Miss Kathleen Moses, a Queen's university student who comes from Niagara Falls, who claims to have been kicked. He might have read the report of Miss Alison Gordon of Edmonton, who said that one of the servicemen at the base who was a friend of hers wrote afterwards apologizing for the rough treatment she was given. He might have read the Globe and Mail of September 17, which quotes Dan Daniels of Montreal, Andre Cardinal of Montreal and Peter Boothroyd of Toronto saying there was beating and brutal treatment of some of those who took part in the demonstration. I do not know whether those statements are accurate or not. I have a letter from a woman in Montreal who participated along with her two daughters, and she said she was thrown in a ditch and so were her two daughters, that servicemen jumped on them, and that she saw people being kicked while they lay on the ground. I do not know whether these statements are accurate but there is one thing I think the house and the country should understand. These were not young roughnecks or juvenile delinquents. In the main they were young people who are pacifists. They came almost directly from the peace camp at Grindstone, Ontario operated by the Society of Friends, or Quakers, and they returned to their camp after the demonstration was over.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I am not a pacifist but I submit that in a democracy every person has a right to be a pacifist and those of us who believe in democracy must preserve the rights of people who do not believe as we do. Voltaire said: "I disagree with what you say but I will defend to the death your right to say it." We must also be prepared to take the same attitude when people take certain action of which we do not approve. If these young people were breaking the law the minister had a clear course of action open to him. He could have had these people arrested and charged with obstructing traffic or disturbing the peace. If found guilty they could have been punished by due process of law, not by policemen, military or otherwise, beating them up. If we are to allow the police to use their judgment as to whether or not persons ought to be abused, we are setting our feet on the slippery path that leads to a police state.
I wrote down what the minister said this afternoon. He said that if any of these young people felt that undue force had been used he would have expected them to lay charges and follow the due process of law as laid down in the constitution. That is the most ridiculous statement I have ever heard from a minister of the crown. How would these young people, university students, set in motion the due process of law? Would they sue the Department of National Defence? Would they obtain a fiat from the Minister of Justice? Where would they get the necessary funds to enable them to prosecute the crown? Surely the minister, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), to whom I appeal, have the responsibility, when people make charges in the public press that there has been brutal mistreatment by military police, to investigate the matter

and I do not mean by having some army or air force officer look into it; I mean by appointing some impartial person or body to determine whether or not these allegations are true.
I am not anxious that anybody should be punished over this. I am anxious that if these statements are true, action should be taken so that such incidents will not happen again and so that military police or any other police be adequately trained and disciplined in order that they will not use abusive methods. Violence always begets violence, and if the crown acquiesces in the use of violence by any of its servants we are asking for the day when other groups, not pacifists but more unruly groups, will begin to think the same methods can be used by them with


impunity. I hope the government will give us a better answer tonight than the one we got this afternoon and I appeal to the government and to the Prime Minister, when he looks over the record of this debate, to institute an impartial and independent investigation in order that the people of Canada may know that there will be no recurrence of any ill treatment whether by military police or by other police who come under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada.

speechtext:
This afternoon, on the orders of the day, I directed to the right hon. Prime Minister a question which met all the requirements, as it was very important, concise and urgent.
As the Prime Minister refused to answer this afternoon, I have deemed it advisable to discuss the matter this evening.
Since the Prime Minister and his parliamentary secretaries are not here, I would therefore ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to answer my question, since he took part in the election campaign.
My question was as follows:
Can the Prime Minister tell us if his government intends to grant subsidies to the numerous cultural centres which are being promised by the Liberal party in the county of Dorchester during the current by-election campaign, and. if so, does he thereby admit that "operation agriculture" having failed in this county, the situation might be remedied through "operation culture"?
Mr. Speaker, I have been prompted to ask this question by the list of innumerable promises which appears daily in the newspapers aimed at the voters who will choose a representative on October 5 next in the counties of Dorchester, Matane, etc.
Never before have we seen in our province an auction similar to the one now in progress in these counties. The shower of promises, of subsidies is such that the people of Dorchester feel swamped; municipal parks

here, sludge plants there, confederation monument elsewhere, and many more still.
One may wonder if the $100 million the Lesage government borrowed from a Social Credit government, that of British Columbia, just before the election, will not be all squandered on highway projects, asphalt and all kinds of gifts for the Dorchester county alone.
People in the county are no fools since we could hear from electors in various ridings comments such as:	"We are getting
buried under asphalt" or "One may wonder if it would not be better for our representative to die every year".
Obviously these people are right since not a single penny had been spent in four years and within four weeks millions are being poured into the county.
But the most dazzling, the most brilliant and the most subtle of all those promises is to build "cultural centres" in almost every parish of the county of Dorchester. Just think, Mr. Speaker, in an entirely rural environment where 60 per cent of the people live from the land, cultural centres are to be built, not in order to show our farmers how to improve their land and pursue their great calling-no, our people in Dorchester are to become little intellectuals, subtle little minds, in a word, they are to become sophisticated.
Mr. Speaker, the most ridiculous aspect in all this election story, which will never be forgotten, is that some good politicians in Ottawa are going to help those auctioneers.
Indeed, we have seen the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) and the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) "Mr. ARDA", both federal ministers, go to that riding and speak in favour of the new co-operative federalism, that is the federalism of election promises. We also heard the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laver-diere) strongly approve the decision to build cultural centres in the county of Dorchester.
Mr. Speaker, as the federal members are all for the building of such cultural centres, the federal government must have given its authorization, or have promised the government of the province of Quebec to subsidize those centres, which are to be centennial projects. As those centres have already been officially announced by the Quebec government in at least two parishes of that county, i.e. in Ste Germaine, for an amount of $100,000, and at St. Prosper for an equal amount, the federal government obviously promised to give those centres to the people.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
This is the answer I should like to receive from the Prime Minister. Did the government grant an amount to the Ste Germaine and St. Prosper parishes or is this promise only eyewash on the part of the Lesage government?
In my question I asked of the Prime Minister: "Does he admit that "operation agriculture" having failed, the situation might be remedied through "operation culture"?
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, agriculture is in a state of depression in our area. That is why the Liberal party does not mention the subject during this campaign; they prefer to take farmers for a ride in the clouds instead of dealing with their problems. It is certainly not ARDA which will save them.
Since Mr. Lesage is so much in favour of co-operative federalism, why does he refuse to request the assistance of the federal Minister of Agriculture to help maple sugar and syrup producers in the province of Quebec whose production was a complete failure last spring?
Since Mr. Lesage said he looks after the problems of all the people of Quebec, why did he hide when 20,000 farmers marched on Quebec city?
Those are points the premier of Quebec and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should explain to voters instead of encouraging the orgy of promises which takes place during these by-elections.
If Mr. Lesage is serious and sincere when he talks of co-operative federalism, he should ask as soon as possible the federal government to help farmers, instead of hiding, or turning a deaf ear to their requests.
Would the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration answer up to a certain point the questions I just put to him?

Mr. Speaker, because of a perhaps all too narrow preoccupation with federal politics and federal policies, I am not directly familiar with the particular local issues important in the provincial byelection now going on in the splendid county of Dorchester. I believe that the Prime Minister was in a somewhat similar position. Moreover, I suspect that when this question first came up this afternoon he and the Speaker concluded that this was a matter primarily within provincial jurisdiction.
Indeed, I am rather surprised to find that this matter is put down for discussion at this hour, and what the hon. gentleman has

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion just said confirms me in my wonderment at its being before us now. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. gentleman is looking for reassurance, and that I can make him rest easier by telling him that there is a well established tradition that Liberals strive to do those things which they promise to try to do. I am sure that in this instance this tradition will prevail.
But, sir, one aspect of the hon. member's question as he put it this afternoon caused some concern. He asked, hypothetically, if in the county of Dorchester agriculture is to be supplanted by culture. He seemed to imply that Dorchester could not sustain both at the
same time. The problem of eastern agriculture is a difficult one. I do not think I should attempt to give my views on it this evening. But I am sure the hon. member did not wish to imply that there was some sort of contradiction between agriculture and culture. I am sure that, while we may disagree as to what good government is, he would agree with me that under good government both sound agriculture and genuine culture can flourish in his fine county.
